title: Every graph is a list of solutions
hook: Is the point (4, 1) on the line 2x - 3y = 5?
insight: A graph is every (x, y) that makes its equation true, so 'on the line' means plug in and check: 2(4) - 3(1) = 5, yes. Read the other way, an intersection is the one point on both lists.
visual: Points rain onto the plane, those that satisfy 2x - 3y = 5 stay ink while the rest fade, and the survivors line up into the line itself; then a second line's survivors overlap the first at one accent point.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Every graph question gets easier once you see this.

title: Cross-multiply without parentheses and you get -3. It's -11
insight: A fraction bar is a parenthesis, so the 5 multiplies all of x + 2: 5x + 10 = 3x - 12 and x = -11. Writing 5x + 2 = 3x - 4 gives the decoy x = -3.
visual: The fraction bars curl up into parentheses around x + 2 and x - 4 as the 5 and the 3 swing across, then each one multiplies both terms.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. A fraction bar is a parenthesis. Remember it.

title: Why you solve equations backwards: socks and shoes
hook: 3x + 5 = 20. Why do you subtract before you divide?
insight: The equation is a recipe done to x: times 3, then plus 5. Undo it in reverse order, minus 5 and then divide by 3, so x = 15/3 = 5.
visual: A dot labeled x passes through two boxes, x3 then +5, and lands on 20, then walks back through -5 and /3 in reverse to land on 5.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Every equation on it unwinds this way.

title: Linear equations in one variable, in 60 seconds
hook: Every one-variable equation on the SAT, in five pictures.
insight: Keep the balance: distribute to every term, clear fractions with the common denominator, gather x on one side, undo in reverse order, then read the ending: x = a number is one solution, 0 = 5 is none, 0 = 0 is every number.
visual: One balance scale carries the whole video: arrows distribute, a x12 stamp clears fractions, x slides to one side, and the last frame splits into three endings: one crossing, two parallel lines, one doubled line.
payoff: the whole linear equations in one variable skill
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Here is every one-variable equation it can ask.

title: Linear functions in 60 seconds
hook: Every SAT linear function question is one sentence: start, then rate.
insight: f(x) = b + mx: b is the value at 0, m is the change per one more unit, a change of k units moves the output by m times k, f(a) = c is the point (a, c), and two points give m as rise over run.
visual: One line on one grid gathers each beat: a dot at the intercept, a staircase for the rate, a stretched k-step triangle, a dot labeled f(a), then a recap stack of five mini-frames.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. All of linear functions, in one minute.

title: Every way the SAT writes a line, in 60 seconds
hook: Slope-intercept, standard, point-slope. One line, three outfits.
insight: y = mx + b shows slope and start, Ax + By = C has slope -A/B and intercepts by cover-up, y - y1 = m(x - x1) builds a line from one point, parallel lines share m, and perpendicular slopes flip and negate.
visual: One line never moves while three equations cycle above it, each lighting the feature it reveals, then a parallel copy slides beside it and a perpendicular one rotates in.
payoff: the whole linear equations in two variables skill
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Every form of a line, in one minute.

skill: Systems of two linear equations in two variables
title: You solved this SAT system right and still got it wrong
hook: 2x + y = 11 and x - y = 1. What is y?
insight: Adding the equations gives 3x = 12, so x = 4, and that 4 sits in the choices. The question asked for y: 4 - y = 1, so y = 3.
visual: The two equations add and the y's cancel, 4 appears and is circled, then struck in blue as the question's last word, y, lights up and 3 resolves.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Solve for x, answer for y. Read the end.

skill: Systems of two linear equations in two variables
title: Systems of equations in 60 seconds
hook: Two lines, three possible endings. Every SAT system in one minute.
insight: The solution is where the lines cross; add or substitute to find it; add the equations when the question wants x + y; same slope with different intercepts means no solution; the same line means infinitely many.
visual: Two lines on one grid act out each beat: they cross, one pivots during elimination, they add to x + y, then slide parallel, then merge, ending on a recap of three mini-frames.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Every system question, in one minute.

title: SAT Algebra in 60 seconds: one straight line, a third of the test
hook: A third of SAT math is one picture: a straight line.
insight: A line is a start plus a constant rate; an equation asks where two lines meet; a system asks it for two equations; parallel means no solution and one shared line means infinitely many; an inequality keeps half the plane.
visual: One line on one grid carries all five beats: a staircase for the rate, a second line crossing it, sliding parallel, merging, then half the plane washing blue, ending on a five-frame recap.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. A third of the math section, in one minute.

title: (x + 3)^2 is not x^2 + 9. Here's the missing piece
hook: Is x plus 3, squared, equal to x squared plus 9?
insight: No: (x + 3)^2 is a square of side x + 3 made of an x^2 piece, a 9 piece and two 3x strips, so it equals x^2 + 6x + 9. At x = 1 that is 16, not 10.
visual: A square of side x + 3 splits into four regions, the two 3x strips light up in blue as the missing terms, and x^2 + 9 is struck.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Don't drop the middle term.

title: FOIL is just the four pieces of a rectangle
hook: Why does x plus 2 times x plus 5 give four terms?
insight: (x + 2)(x + 5) is a rectangle x + 2 tall and x + 5 wide, and cutting it along x gives four pieces: x^2, 5x, 2x and 10. So it equals x^2 + 7x + 10.
visual: A rectangle with sides x + 2 and x + 5 gets sliced into a 2-by-2 grid, each piece fills in with its area, and the two x strips merge into 7x.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Never forget a FOIL term again.

title: Why two years of 10% growth is 21%, not 20%
hook: Grow 10%, then 10% again. Why is the total 21%, not 20%?
insight: The second 10% applies to the already-grown amount, so 1.1 times 1.1 = 1.21. As a square of side 1.1, the extra is two 0.1 strips plus a tiny 0.01 corner: growth on the growth.
visual: A unit square stretches to 1.1 by 1.1, two thin 0.1 strips appear along its sides, and the small 0.01 corner square glows blue as the hidden extra 1%.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. One tiny square explains compound growth.

title: Why the vertex of a parabola is at x = -b/(2a)
hook: Where does negative b over 2a actually come from?
insight: Changing c only slides the parabola up and down, so drop it: ax^2 + bx = x(ax + b) has zeros at 0 and -b/a. The vertex sits halfway between them, at x = -b/(2a).
visual: The parabola slides vertically as c changes while its axis stays fixed, it stops where c = 0 and crosses at 0 and -b/a, and the midpoint lights up.
payoff: Finding the vertex from standard form
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. The vertex formula, derived in one slide.

title: Per cent literally means per hundred. Watch 7% of 300 build itself
hook: What is 7% of 300? Read the word percent slowly.
insight: Per cent is Latin for per hundred, so 7% means 7 out of every 100. 300 holds three hundreds, so 7% of 300 is 7 + 7 + 7 = 21.
visual: Three 10-by-10 grids of 100 squares sit side by side, 7 squares in each light up blue, then the 21 lit squares slide together into one row.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Percent questions get easy once you read the word.

title: SAT Percents in 60 seconds
hook: Every SAT percent question is one of five moves.
insight: Percent means per hundred; of means multiply; a change is one multiplier, 1 + r or 1 - r; successive changes multiply; and reverse problems divide by the multiplier.
visual: Five beats on one bar: a 100-square grid, an of-to-times swap, the bar stretching by 1.2, two multipliers chaining, and the bar dividing back by 0.8, ending in a five-row recap.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Here is every percent move you need.

title: Why a pyramid is one third of a box
hook: Why does a pyramid's volume have a one third in it?
insight: Three identical pyramids, each with one face of a cube as its base and a shared corner as its tip, fill the cube exactly. So a pyramid is 1/3 x base x height, and a cone is 1/3 of its cylinder.
visual: Three wireframe pyramids rotate in from different sides and lock together into one cube, then a cone pours into a cylinder three times to fill it.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Three pyramids make one cube. Watch.

title: Fill a cone glass to half its height. How full is it?
hook: A cone-shaped glass is filled to half its height. What fraction is full?
insight: Only 1/8, not 1/2. The water is a cone similar to the glass with scale factor 1/2, and volume scales by k^3 = 1/8.
visual: Water rises to the midline of a wireframe cone glass, the water cone lifts out and shrinks onto the full cone, and eight copies stack to fill it.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Volume scales by k cubed. This glass proves it.

title: Tear off a triangle's corners and watch
hook: Draw any triangle. Tear off its three corners. What do they make?
insight: A straight line, which is 180 degrees, for every triangle. A line through the top vertex parallel to the base shows why: the base angles reappear there as alternate angles.
visual: Three corners tear off along jagged arcs and glide together at one point into a straight line, then the triangle reshapes and the corners line up again.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Tear the corners off any triangle. Always 180.

title: Why 3^2 + 4^2 = 5^2, with one tilted square
hook: Why is 3 squared plus 4 squared exactly 5 squared?
insight: Put a tilted 5 by 5 square inside a 7 by 7 box: the box is 49 and the four corner triangles are 6 each, so the square is 25. Rearrange the same triangles and the leftover space is a 3 by 3 plus a 4 by 4.
visual: Four 3-4-5 triangles slide around inside the 7 by 7 box, and the blue space they leave changes from one tilted 5 by 5 square into a 3 by 3 and a 4 by 4.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. One sliding picture proves Pythagoras.

title: Why a circle's area is pi r^2
hook: Why is the area of a circle pi r squared?
insight: Cut the circle into thin wedges and lay them tip to tail: they form a near-rectangle with height r and length half the circumference, pi r. Area = pi r x r = pi r^2.
visual: A circle cut into 16 wedges unrolls into a row of alternating wedges, then 32 and 64 wedges flatten it into a clean rectangle labeled pi r by r.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Unroll a circle and pi r squared appears.

title: The circle equation is just Pythagoras
hook: Why is (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2 a circle?
insight: Every point on the circle is r from the center, and its horizontal gap x - h and vertical gap y - k are the legs of a right triangle with hypotenuse r. The equation is Pythagoras for every point at once.
visual: A point travels around the circle dragging a right triangle back to the center, its legs labeled x - h and y - k and its hypotenuse fixed at r.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. The circle equation is a triangle spinning.

title: SAT Algebra in 60 seconds: one line, 13-15 questions
hook: Thirteen to fifteen SAT questions come from five pictures of one line.
insight: Beats: a line is a start plus a rate (b and m in context), solving is where two lines meet, parallel lines mean no solution and the same line means infinitely many, adding equations swings a line onto the answer, and an inequality keeps half the plane. That covers all five Algebra skills.
visual: One shared grid: a staircase climbs a line, a second line crosses it, tilts parallel so the crossing runs off the page, merges onto it, then half the plane floods with accentWash; nav 'line · system · solutions · inequality'.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. A third of the math section is this one line.

title: SAT Advanced Math in 60 seconds
hook: The hardest third of SAT math is one curve, read five ways.
insight: Beats: equivalent expressions draw the same graph so you match coefficients, factored form puts the zeros on the axis, the vertex sits halfway between the zeros at x = -b/2a, the discriminant b^2 - 4ac counts crossings, and a(1 + r)^t multiplies where a line adds. Those five cover all three Advanced Math skills.
visual: One parabola stays on the page while its formula morphs from standard to factored to vertex form, zeros and vertex light in accent, the parabola slides up through the axis with a crossing counter 2-1-0, then an exponential peels away from it.
payoff: the Advanced Math questions in both modules
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days out. A third of the math questions live on this one curve.

title: Two lines, three endings: SAT systems in 60 seconds
hook: Two lines, three possible endings. That's every SAT systems question.
insight: Beats: the solution is the crossing point; elimination adds the equations so a new line swings through that point until it reads x = answer; when they ask for x + y, one add or subtract finishes it; equal slopes with different intercepts mean no solution; identical lines mean infinitely many.
visual: Two lines cross with the point in accent, a third line pivots through that point as the multiplier changes until it stands vertical, then one line tilts parallel and the crossing slides off the page, and finally it slides onto the other and they merge.
payoff: Systems of two linear equations in two variables
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Every systems question on it ends one of three ways.

title: Equivalent expressions in 60 seconds: same graph, every x
hook: Two expressions that look nothing alike. Same graph. That's the skill.
insight: Beats: distribute to every term, minus signs included; factor out the shared piece; x^2 - 9 = (x - 3)(x + 3) because a square with a corner cut out rearranges into a rectangle; x^(3/2) = x·sqrt(x) because exponents count factors; and 'equivalent for all x' means match the coefficients term by term.
visual: Two different formulas draw two curves that slide until they lie exactly on top of each other, an x-by-x square loses its 3-by-3 corner and rearranges into an (x + 3)-by-(x - 3) rectangle, and matching coefficients light in pairs.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Every equivalent-expression question is one graph drawn twice.

title: Nonlinear functions in 60 seconds: the biggest SAT skill
hook: The single biggest skill in SAT math comes down to three curves.
insight: Beats: a parabola's vertex is its maximum or minimum and sits at x = -b/2a; factored form shows the zeros and vertex form shows the turn; a(1 + r)^t starts at a and multiplies by 1 + r each step, so 0.85 means 15% off; f(x - 3) + 2 moves right 3 and up 2; and f(0) is the starting value of any model.
visual: A parabola, an exponential and a shifted copy share one grid: the vertex dot drops a dashed guide to -b/2a, the exponential stamps x1.05 at each tick, then the parabola glides right 3 and up 2 while its inside label reads x - 3.
payoff: Nonlinear functions, the largest skill in the question bank
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. The biggest skill on the test, in one minute.

title: SAT percents in 60 seconds: every one is a multiplier
hook: 30% of 60. Up 20% then down 20%. 400% more. One move.
insight: Beats: 'percent of' multiplies (0.3 x 60 = 18); up p% is x(1 + p/100), so up 400% is x5, not x4; successive changes multiply (1.2 x 0.8 = 0.96, a 4% loss); percent change is the change over the original; and a reverse percent divides ($80 after 20% off was 80/0.8 = $100).
visual: One bar carries the whole video: it shades 30%, stretches by x1.2 then shrinks by x0.8 to fall short of the start line, grows to five copies for +400%, and finally un-shrinks from $80 back to $100.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Every percent question on it is one multiplication.

title: SAT right triangles and trig in 60 seconds
hook: Why does sine only depend on the angle? Everything follows from that.
insight: Beats: Pythagoras with the triples 3-4-5, 5-12-13 and 8-15-17; sine, cosine and tangent are fixed because same-angle right triangles are similar; sin x = cos(90 - x); a 30-60-90 is half an equilateral (x, x sqrt3, 2x) and a 45-45-90 is half a square (s, s, s sqrt2); and a given ratio like sin = 3/5 means sides 3k and 5k.
visual: Right triangles of every size share one angle while the ratio readout never moves, the angle label hops to the other corner and sine becomes cosine, an equilateral triangle splits down the middle, and a square splits along its diagonal.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Most trig questions are hard ones; these five facts carry them.

title: Geometry class in 60 seconds: everything the SAT kept
hook: A whole year of Geometry. The SAT kept five pictures.
insight: Beats: parallel-line angles and the 180 in every triangle; congruence and similarity shortcuts (SSS, SAS, ASA, AA) with sides scaling by k; Pythagoras with 3-4-5 and 5-12-13; area and volume with the 1/3 for cones and pyramids; and circles with arcs as fractions and tangents at right angles. No proofs.
visual: Nav 'Alg 1 · Alg 2 · Geo · Trig' with Geo underlined; a transversal splits angles into two colors, two triangles slide and scale onto each other, a 3-4-5 triangle grows squares on its sides, three pyramids fill a cube, and a tangent meets a radius at a right angle.
payoff: Geometry questions, mapped to the class you took
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Your whole geometry year, cut to what it tests.

title: Every SAT math trap in 60 seconds
hook: The SAT reuses the same five traps. Here they are.
insight: Beats: answering the wrong quantity (x when they asked for 2x); the wrong percent base (the new value instead of the original); mixing up no solution and infinitely many; using r^2 or the diameter as the radius; and scaling area by k instead of k^2. Each is shown, struck in blue, and fixed.
visual: Five tiny problems stack down the page; each shows the tempting wrong answer in ink, a blue strike sweeps through it, and the right answer slides in, then all five collapse into a checklist.
payoff: the repeat traps across all four domains
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. These five traps show up on nearly every SAT.

title: Quadratics in 60 seconds: three forms, one parabola
hook: Three formulas, one parabola. Each one gives you something free.
insight: Beats: factored form a(x - r)(x - s) shows the zeros; vertex form a(x - h)^2 + k shows the turning point; standard form ax^2 + bx + c shows the y-intercept c; the vertex sits halfway between the zeros; and the quadratic formula is that midpoint, -b/2a, plus or minus a distance.
visual: One parabola never moves while three formulas cycle above it, each lighting its free feature in accent: two zeros, a vertex, a y-intercept; then two equal arrows reach out from the axis of symmetry to the roots.
payoff: quadratic questions across both Advanced Math skills
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Quadratics run all through it; here are all three forms.

title: Every SAT word problem is one of five sentences
hook: A gym, a bank account, a recipe, tickets, a discount. Five sentences.
insight: Beats: 'a start plus a rate' is y = b + mx; 'grows by r percent each period' is a(1 + r)^t; 'the same ratio' is y = kx through the origin; 'two kinds of items, a count and a total' is a system; and 'percent off, then tax' is a chain of multipliers. Name the sentence and the equation writes itself.
visual: Five story cards drop onto the page and each folds into its picture: a staircase line, a curve stamping x(1 + r), a ray from the origin, two crossing lines, and a bar shrinking then growing.
payoff: modeling and interpretation questions in every domain
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Every word problem on it is one of these five.

title: How the SAT's adaptive second module works, in one diagram
hook: Why did your second math module feel harder than the first?
insight: Module 1 mixes easy, medium and hard questions for everyone; how you do on it routes you to an easier or a harder Module 2. Each 22-question, 35-minute module runs from easiest to hardest, and the harder Module 2 is the route to the top of the scale, so a harder second module is usually a good sign.
visual: A flow diagram draws itself: one Module 1 box with a difficulty ramp inside, a fork, an upper harder Module 2 box and a lower easier one, and a dot traveling the upper path while a mono score scale stretches higher along that branch.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Know how Module 2 gets chosen before you sit down.

title: Your wrong answer is in the choices on purpose
hook: A circle's area is 36 pi. Its diameter: 6, 12, 18 or 36?
insight: 12: r^2 = 36, so r = 6 and the diameter is 12. Each wrong choice is a predictable slip, 6 is the radius, 36 is r^2 and 18 is half of 36, so finding your number among the choices proves nothing; check what was asked.
visual: The circle with area 36 pi draws, the radius 6 inks and then doubles across the circle into a diameter of 12 in accent, while the choices 6, 18 and 36 each get a small gray tag naming the slip that produces them.
payoff: every multiple-choice question, r versus d versus r^2 especially
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days out. The wrong answers are built from your likeliest slips.

title: Why the same number right can give different SAT scores
hook: Same number of right answers. Different math scores. How?
insight: The digital SAT is scored with item response theory: College Board says your score depends on which questions you got right, including their difficulty, not just how many, so two students with the same count can earn different section scores.
visual: Two rows of 44 tiles fill with the same number of check marks in different places, the tiles shade from light to dark by difficulty, and a mono score readout above each row settles at a different number.
urgent_hook: Scores for {test} are out. Here is why your count of right answers isn't your score.

title: Slope and sine are the same triangle
hook: Why is slope the same everywhere on a line? Same reason sine works.
insight: Every slope triangle on a line has the same angles, so the triangles are similar and rise/run never changes; every right triangle with a 30 degree angle is similar too, so opposite/hypotenuse is always 1/2. Slope is literally the tangent of the line's angle.
visual: Slope triangles of every size slide along a line and scale into each other under a frozen ratio readout, then the line rotates to 30 degrees and the readout relabels from 'slope' to 'tan 30 = 0.577'.
payoff: slope from two points and trig ratios
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Slope and trig are one idea; see it once.

title: Why (x + 3)^2 is not x^2 + 9, in one picture
hook: Is (x + 3) squared equal to x^2 + 9?
insight: No: a square with side x + 3 holds an x^2 square, a 9 square and two x-by-3 strips, so (x + 3)^2 = x^2 + 6x + 9. The 6x is the area everyone forgets.
visual: A square of side x + 3 splits into four regions; x^2 + 9 is inked and struck in blue as the x^2 and 9 pieces light, then the two 3x strips glow in accent and slide together into one 6x bar.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. This squaring trap costs points every test.

title: Up 20%, then down 15%. The net change is not +5%.
hook: A price rises 20%, then falls 15%. What's the net change?
insight: A 2% gain: percent changes multiply, 1.2 x 0.85 = 1.02. That same multiplication is every growth model too, since 5% a year for t years is x1.05^t.
visual: A bar stretches by x1.2 and shrinks by x0.85 to land 2% above the start line with +5% struck in blue; then the same stretch repeats at each tick of a timeline and the bar tops trace an exponential curve.
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Percents multiply; this is the trap that proves it.

title: Why x - 3 always means +3 on the SAT
hook: (x - 3) is a factor, a center, a vertex, a shift. Why +3?
insight: Each one asks where x - 3 becomes zero, which is x = 3: the zero of the factor (x - 3), the center of (x - 3)^2 + y^2 = r^2, the vertex of (x - 3)^2 + k, and f(x - 3) shifted right 3. The minus sign is pointing at +3.
visual: The chunk x - 3 appears in four formulas stacked down the page, and under each a dashed guide drops to x = 3 where the chunk is zero: a crossing, a circle's center, a vertex, and a curve sliding right.
payoff: sign errors in zeros, circles, vertex form and shifts
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. One sign rule fixes four kinds of questions.

title: The distance formula and the circle equation are both Pythagoras
hook: How far is (1, 2) from (7, 10)?
insight: 10: the right triangle between the points has legs 6 and 8, so the distance is sqrt(36 + 64) = 10. Let the far point roam while that distance stays 10 and it traces the circle (x - 1)^2 + (y - 2)^2 = 100.
visual: A right triangle drops between (1, 2) and (7, 10) with legs 6 and 8 and hypotenuse 10; then the far vertex slides around keeping the hypotenuse at 10, tracing a full circle.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Two formulas, one triangle; stop memorizing both.

title: One minus sign turns x = -2 into x = -10
hook: 3 - 2(x - 4) = 15. What is x?
insight: The -2 multiplies both terms inside, so -2 times -4 is +8: 11 - 2x = 15 and x = -2. Writing -8 instead of +8 gives the decoy x = -10.
visual: Two arrows arc from the -2 to x and to -4, the second product inks as -8, is struck in blue and flips to +8, and the balance settles at x = -2.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. This one minus sign costs points every test.

title: The SAT asked for 6x + 10. The trap answer is 4
hook: If 3x + 5 = 17, what is 6x + 10?
insight: 6x + 10 is exactly two copies of 3x + 5, so it equals 2 times 17 = 34. Solving gives x = 4, the decoy sitting in the choices.
visual: The expression 6x + 10 splits into two stacked copies of 3x + 5, each copy collapses to 17, and they add to 34 in blue.
urgent_hook: The SAT is in {days} days. It will ask for an expression, not x.

title: In 5 years, both people get older. Don't forget one
hook: Sam is 3 times Ana's age; in 5 years, twice. How old is Ana?
insight: Both ages grow by 5: 3a + 5 = 2(a + 5), so 3a + 5 = 2a + 10 and a = 5. Adding 5 to Sam only, 3a + 5 = 2a, gives Ana an impossible age of -5.
visual: Two bars, Ana's and Sam's three times as tall, both grow by the same 5-unit block, and Sam's bar settles at exactly twice Ana's: 20 and 10.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Age the whole story, not one person.

title: Count the boxes and you get slope 2. It's 5
hook: The y-axis counts by 5s, the x-axis by 2s. What's the slope?
insight: Read coordinates from the tick labels, not the boxes: the line goes through (0, 5) and (2, 15), so the slope is 10/2 = 5, not the 2 you get by counting boxes.
visual: Boxes are tallied up and across to give 2, which is struck in blue, then the gridlines relabel with their tick values and the slope triangle reads 10 over 2.
payoff: matching a line to its graph
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Read the axis labels before you count.

title: f(k) = 21 is not f(21)
hook: f(x) = 4x - 7. If f(k) = 21, what is k?
insight: f(k) = 21 says the output is 21, so solve 4k - 7 = 21: k = 7. Plugging 21 in gives f(21) = 77, the trap.
visual: A function machine takes 21 at its input, which is struck in blue, then runs in reverse: 21 enters at the output, +7 makes 28, /4 makes 7.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Input or output? Decide before you plug in.

title: 120 members in month 3. That is not the starting number
hook: 120 members in month 3, 180 in month 7. Write the linear model.
insight: Slope = 60/4 = 15 members per month; walk back 3 months from 120: 120 - 45 = 75. So M = 75 + 15t, not 120 + 15t.
visual: Two dots sit at t = 3 and t = 7, and the line through them extends left in three 15-member steps down until it meets the y-axis at 75 in blue.
payoff: building a linear model from context
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. A data point is not the intercept unless t = 0.

title: Why "$3.50 for the first mile" hides a $1.25 fee
hook: 3.50 + 2.25(m - 1). Why is that the same as 1.25 + 2.25m?
insight: Expanding gives 3.50 - 2.25 + 2.25m = 1.25 + 2.25m: the first mile is really a $1.25 pickup fee plus the normal $2.25. That is why the equivalent answer choice looks nothing like the story.
visual: The first $3.50 block splits into a $1.25 sliver and a regular $2.25 block, which slides into line with the others so every mile looks identical.
payoff: choosing the equivalent model among choices
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. The equivalent form hides a fee. Find it.

title: x goes up by 4. Don't plug in 4
hook: y = 3.5x + 12. x increases by 4. How much does y increase?
insight: The 12 never changes, so only the slope matters: 3.5 times 4 = 14. Plugging in x = 4 gives 26, the trap.
visual: A slope triangle stretches along the line from 1 step to 4 steps wide, its height growing 3.5 at a time to 14, while the intercept stays pinned.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Change in y is slope times change in x.

title: Why the slope of Ax + By = C is -A/B
hook: 4x + 6y = 18. Where does the minus in the slope come from?
insight: Solving for y moves 4x across the equals sign, which flips its sign: 6y = -4x + 18, so y = -(4/6)x + 3. The slope is -A/B = -2/3.
visual: The 4x term slides across the equals sign and its plus turns to a minus mid-flight, then everything divides by 6 and -2/3 lands in blue.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. See why -A/B, then never forget it.

skill: Systems of two linear equations in two variables
title: Substitute without parentheses and x comes out 34/7
hook: y = 2x - 1 and 3x + 2y = 33. What is x?
insight: The whole expression replaces y, so 3x + 2(2x - 1) = 33 gives 7x - 2 = 33, x = 5 and y = 9. Writing 3x + 4x - 1 = 33 drops part of the product and gives 34/7.
visual: The expression 2x - 1 lifts out of the first equation, wraps itself in parentheses mid-flight, and drops into the y slot so the 2 multiplies both terms.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Substitute with parentheses, every time.

skill: Systems of two linear equations in two variables
title: No solution: find k. The flipped ratio gives 20. It's 5
hook: 3x+ky=8 and 6x+10y=5 have no solution. What is k?
insight: No solution means the left sides are proportional but the constants are not: 3/6 = k/10, so k = 5. Since 8/5 is not 1/2, the lines are parallel, not identical.
visual: The line 3x + ky = 8 pivots as k slides, its crossing point with the fixed line runs off the page, and at k = 5 the two lines lie parallel with a gap.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. This no-solution system is a hard-module favorite.

skill: Systems of two linear equations in two variables
title: This "no solution" answer is actually infinitely many
hook: 2x+3y=7 and ax+by=21. Which a and b give no solution?
insight: a = 6, b = 9 makes 6x + 9y = 21, exactly 3 times the first equation: the same line, infinitely many solutions. a = 4, b = 6 gives 2x + 3y = 10.5, parallel to 2x + 3y = 7: no solution.
visual: The first line draws; the choice (6, 9) lands exactly on top of it and merges, struck in blue, then (4, 6) settles parallel beside it with a visible gap.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Parallel or identical? Check the constants.

skill: Systems of two linear equations in two variables
title: Why the crossing point solves both equations at once
hook: Why is the answer to a system where the two lines cross?
insight: Every point on a line makes its equation true, and only the crossing point is on both lines. At (4, 3), 2x + y = 11 and x - y = 1 are both true.
visual: A dot walks along 2x + y = 11 with a live readout of x - y beside it, ticking 7, 4, 1, and the readout lands on exactly 1 at the crossing.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. The crossing point is the answer. Here's why.

skill: Systems of two linear equations in two variables
title: "Twice as many adults as children": a = 2c or 2a = c?
hook: Twice as many adults as children. a = 2c or 2a = c?
insight: Test with numbers: 10 children means 20 adults, so a = 2c. Writing 2a = c in word order would give 5 adults, the reversed trap.
visual: The sentence's words drop into an equation in reading order as 2a = c, a row of 10 child icons and 20 adult icons appears, and the equation is struck in blue and rebuilt as a = 2c.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Test your equation with real numbers first.

skill: Linear inequalities in one or two variables
title: You can afford 10.6 rides. The answer is not 11
hook: $100 budget, $15 entry, $8 per ride. Most rides?
insight: 15 + 8r <= 100 gives r <= 10.625, and "at most" means round down: 10 rides cost $95, while 11 would cost $103.
visual: Ride tickets stack up beside a $100 ceiling line, the tenth fits under it, and the eleventh pokes through the ceiling and is struck in blue.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Round down when the budget is a ceiling.

skill: Linear inequalities in one or two variables
title: 45.25 rounds to 45. The answer is 46
hook: The club has $138, earns $8 per shirt, needs at least $500. Fewest shirts?
insight: 138 + 8s >= 500 gives s >= 45.25, and 45 shirts fall short at $498. "At least" means round up: 46 shirts reach $506.
visual: A savings bar climbs in $8 steps toward a $500 line, stalls at $498 after 45 shirts, and the 46th step crosses the line in blue.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. At least means round up, even from .25.

title: The 5 algebra patterns behind the hardest SAT questions
hook: Retaking? Five algebra patterns keep showing up in the hardest questions.
insight: No-solution systems (same ratio, different constant), each-additional models (m - 1), graphs of f(x) + k (subtract k), greatest whole number (round by the story), and two-constraint maximums (minimize the other variable).
visual: Chapter nav 1 ratio, 2 m-1, 3 shift, 4 round, 5 corner underlines each beat as one mini-diagram per pattern draws, then all five stack into a recap.
urgent_hook: Scores are out. If {test} is your retake, start with these five patterns.

title: If 5x + 3y = 3, what is 32^x times 8^y?
hook: 5x + 3y = 3. What is 32^x times 8^y?
insight: Rewrite both bases as powers of 2: 32^x times 8^y = 2^(5x) times 2^(3y) = 2^(5x + 3y) = 2^3 = 8. You never need x or y.
visual: 32 and 8 dissolve into 2^5 and 2^3, the exponents slide together into 5x + 3y, which lights up as the given 3, and 2^3 resolves to 8 in accent.
payoff: Same-base rewriting linked to a linear condition
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. This exponent question looks impossible until you see this.

title: sqrt(50) + sqrt(8) is not sqrt(58)
hook: What is the square root of 50 plus the square root of 8?
insight: Pull out perfect squares: sqrt(50) = 5sqrt(2) and sqrt(8) = 2sqrt(2), which are like terms. The sum is 7sqrt(2), about 9.9, while sqrt(58) is only about 7.6.
visual: 50 splits into 25 times 2 and 8 into 4 times 2, the 5 and the 2 step out of their roots, and two stacks of sqrt(2) join into seven while sqrt(58) is struck.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. This radical trap fools almost everyone the first time.

title: sqrt(9 + 16) is not 3 + 4
hook: Is the square root of 9 plus 16 equal to 7?
insight: No: sqrt(9 + 16) = sqrt(25) = 5. Roots split over multiplication, sqrt(ab) = sqrt(a)sqrt(b), but never over addition.
visual: A 3-by-3 and a 4-by-4 square of tiles sit side by side, their 25 tiles rearrange into a single 5-by-5 square, and the 7 is struck in blue.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Roots never split over a plus sign. Remember this picture.

title: Subtract 3x^2 - 5x + 2 FROM x^2 + 4x - 7. Watch the order
hook: Subtract 3x squared minus 5x plus 2 from x squared plus 4x minus 7.
insight: "From" means it goes second: (x^2 + 4x - 7) - (3x^2 - 5x + 2). The minus hits every term, giving -2x^2 + 9x - 9.
visual: The two polynomials swap places under the word from, the minus sign sweeps across the second parentheses flipping each sign in blue, and like terms slide into columns.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. This subtraction trap costs easy points.

skill: Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables
title: x^2 = 6x. Dividing by x deletes an answer
hook: Solve x squared equals 6x. Is the answer just 6?
insight: Dividing by x silently assumes x is not 0. Move everything to one side and factor instead: x(x - 6) = 0, so x = 0 or x = 6.
visual: Both sides get divided by x and a hidden solution drops off the page, then the step rewinds, x^2 - 6x factors, and the graph shows crossings at 0 and 6.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Never divide by x. Here's what it costs.

skill: Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables
title: x(x - 3) = 10 does not mean x = 10
hook: If x times x minus 3 equals 10, what is the positive solution?
insight: The zero-product rule only works when the product is 0. Move the 10 over and factor: x^2 - 3x - 10 = (x - 5)(x + 2) = 0, so the positive solution is 5.
visual: The tempting split, x = 10 or x - 3 = 10, gets struck in blue, the 10 slides across to make 0, and the trinomial factors into (x - 5)(x + 2).
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. The zero-product rule needs a zero. Always.

skill: Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables
title: 2x^2 + 4x = c - 3 has exactly one solution. Find c
hook: 2x squared plus 4x equals c minus 3 has exactly one solution. Find c.
insight: Move everything to one side first: 2x^2 + 4x + (3 - c) = 0. Exactly one solution means b^2 - 4ac = 0, so 16 - 8(3 - c) = 0 and c = 1.
visual: The c - 3 slides across the equals sign and flips to 3 - c, the parabola lowers until it just touches the x-axis, and a discriminant counter reads 0.
payoff: Exactly one solution with a constant
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Rearrange before the discriminant. Always.

skill: Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables
title: Why 3x^2 + 7x - 2 = 0 must have two solutions
hook: How many solutions does 3x squared plus 7x minus 2 have? Instantly.
insight: If a and c have opposite signs, the parabola opens up but crosses the y-axis below zero, at -2, so it must cross the x-axis twice. In b^2 - 4ac, the -4ac is then positive, so the discriminant is too.
visual: The parabola's y-intercept dot sits at -2 below the axis, its arms sweep upward, and two crossings light up in blue on either side.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Count the solutions before you compute anything.

skill: Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables
title: Four ways to solve any SAT quadratic in 60 seconds
hook: Factor, square root, complete the square, formula. Which one when? 60 seconds.
insight: Factor when the numbers are friendly, take square roots when there is no x term, complete the square when b is even or you want the vertex, and use the formula or Desmos for everything else. Every method lands on the same crossings.
visual: One parabola stays on the page while four solution methods take turns above it, each ending on the same two crossing points lit in blue, then a recap card.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Four methods, one minute, every quadratic covered.

skill: Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables
title: Every nonlinear equation on the SAT in 60 seconds
hook: Quadratic, radical, rational, absolute value, exponential. Every one, in 60 seconds.
insight: Quadratics: set to zero and factor; radicals: isolate, square, check; rationals: clear denominators and drop excluded values. Absolute values split into plus and minus, and exponentials match bases.
visual: Five equations appear in a column, each one's graph pair draws beside it with the intersections lit, and the fake roots fade as a recap card forms.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Five equation types, one minute, one page.

title: The y-intercept of y = 4(3)^x + 2 is not 4
hook: What is the y-intercept of y = 4(3)^x + 2?
insight: Plug in x = 0: 3^0 = 1, so y = 4 + 2 = 6. The coefficient is the intercept only when nothing is added outside the power.
visual: A vertical probe slides to x = 0, the power 3^x collapses to 1, and the curve's crossing on the y-axis lights up at 6 while 4 is struck.
urgent_hook: {test} is today. This question type shows up on nearly every test.

title: Why the minimum of (x - 3)^2 + 5 is exactly 5
hook: Why is the smallest value of x minus 3, squared, plus 5 exactly 5?
insight: A square is never negative, so (x - 3)^2 is at least 0 and reaches 0 only at x = 3. Add 5 and the smallest output is 5, which is why vertex form shows the vertex.
visual: A square tile labeled (x - 3)^2 shrinks to nothing as x slides to 3, the output readout falls to 5 and stops, and the parabola's vertex lights at (3, 5).
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Why vertex form hands you the minimum.

title: SAT exponential functions in 60 seconds
hook: Every SAT exponential function question, in 60 seconds.
insight: a is the value at time 0, the base is 1 plus the rate, and the exponent counts periods. Tables show constant ratios, and changing units means substituting into the exponent.
visual: One curve y = a times b^t stays on the page while each part of the formula lights up in turn: the intercept, the base, a ticking exponent, a ratio table and a unit change.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Every exponential idea on one page.

title: Every SAT factoring move in 60 seconds
hook: Every factoring move the SAT asks for, in 60 seconds.
insight: Pull out the greatest common factor first, find two numbers for trinomials, split a^2 - b^2 into (a + b)(a - b), and group four terms in pairs. Check any factor by plugging in its zero.
visual: One block of tiles is regrouped four ways, as a shared strip, a rectangle, a square with a corner cut out and two paired pieces, ending in a recap grid.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Every factoring move, in one minute.

title: A $50 shirt goes up 20%, then down 20%. It's not $50
hook: A $50 shirt goes up 20%, then down 20%. What does it cost now?
insight: The 20% off is taken from $60, not $50, so it removes $12 and leaves $48. In multipliers, 1.2 x 0.8 = 0.96: a 4% loss.
visual: A $50 bar grows a blue $10 block to $60, then a $12 slice is cut from the taller bar and it settles $2 below the dashed original line while the struck $50 fades.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. This is the most common percent trap. Skip it.

title: A is 25% more than B. So B is 25% less than A, right?
hook: A is 25% more than B. B is what percent less than A?
insight: Percent change divides by the starting value, and the start switches sides. If B = 4 then A = 5: going up, 1 is 25% of 4; going down, the same 1 is only 20% of 5. The answer is 20%.
visual: A 4-block bar and a 5-block bar sit side by side; the extra blue block is measured against 4 blocks as 25%, then the base outline slides to 5 blocks and the label shrinks to 20%.
payoff: percent change and p% greater than
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Percent greater than is a favorite hard-module trap.

title: A price goes up p%, then down p%, and ends 9% lower. Find p
hook: A price rises p%, then falls p%, and ends 9% lower. What is p?
insight: The multipliers give (1 + r)(1 - r) = 1 - r^2, so up-then-down by the same percent always loses exactly r squared. 1 - r^2 = 0.91 gives r = 0.3, so p = 30.
visual: A unit square becomes a (1 + r)-by-(1 - r) rectangle; the new right strip rotates up to refill the cut top strip but falls one r-by-r square short, and that missing corner turns blue as the loss r^2.
payoff: successive percent changes with an unknown rate
urgent_hook: Retaking on {date}? This up-then-down percent question lives in the hard module.

skill: Ratios, rates, proportional relationships, and units
title: How many square inches are in 3 square feet? Not 36
hook: How many square inches are in 3 square feet?
insight: A square foot is 12 inches by 12 inches, so it holds 144 square inches, not 12. 3 square feet is 3 x 144 = 432 square inches.
visual: A 1-foot square is ruled into a 12-by-12 grid, the cell counter runs up to 144, and three such squares line up as the struck 36 gives way to 432.
urgent_hook: Retaking on {date}? Squared units are a hard-module favorite. Fix this one.

skill: One-variable data: distributions and measures of center and spread
title: SAT Statistics in 60 seconds
hook: Five pictures answer every SAT question about one list of data.
insight: The mean is the balance point, the median is the middle by count, an outlier drags the mean but barely moves the median, standard deviation is the typical distance from the mean, and a box plot cuts the data into quarters.
visual: One dot plot transforms through five beats, a fulcrum, a middle marker, an outlier sliding away, distance sticks, and a box plot forming, ending in a five-line recap.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Every one-variable statistics idea, in one minute.

title: SAT Probability in 60 seconds
hook: Every SAT probability question is a fraction. Only the denominator changes.
insight: Probability is favorable over total; given shrinks the total to one row or column; or adds the groups minus their overlap; and for independent events multiplies; and an expected count is probability times the total.
visual: One two-way table carries every beat, a cell over the grand total, a column fading to its subtotal, two overlapping regions, an area square for and, and a probability chip scaling into a count, ending in a recap.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Every probability question you'll see, in 60 seconds.

title: This parallelogram question fools almost everyone
hook: Base 10, slanted side 5, height 4. What is the area?
insight: Area uses the perpendicular height, not the slanted side: 10 x 4 = 40, not 10 x 5 = 50. Cut the triangle off one end and slide it to the other, and the shape is a 10 by 4 rectangle.
visual: The product 10 x 5 is inked and struck in blue, then the left triangle detaches, glides across and snaps onto the right end, turning the parallelogram into a rectangle while the area chip reads 40.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Never multiply by the slanted side.

title: Cut a corner out of a rectangle. The perimeter stays the same
hook: An 8 by 6 rectangle loses a 2 by 2 corner. Perimeter?
insight: Still 28, not 24: the notch removes 2 + 2 of outer edge but adds 2 + 2 of inner edge. The perimeter equals the full rectangle's, 2(8 + 6) = 28.
visual: The two inner edges of the notch fold outward like hinges and rebuild the missing corner, while the perimeter counter never changes.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. A notched corner keeps the perimeter.

title: A cone plus a sphere fills a cylinder exactly
hook: Why is a sphere's volume 4/3 pi r^3?
insight: A cylinder of radius r and height 2r holds 2pi r^3. The cone inside it is one third, 2/3 pi r^3, and the sphere is exactly the other two thirds, 4/3 pi r^3.
visual: A cone and a sphere of the same radius pour their water into a cylinder of height 2r, the cone filling one third and the sphere topping it off exactly to the brim.
payoff: Sphere volume from the reference sheet
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. The sphere formula is two thirds of a cylinder.

title: The radius is not 16
hook: A cylinder has volume 48pi and height 3. What is its radius?
insight: Divide out the height: r^2 = 48 / 3 = 16, so r = 4. Answering 16 stops one step early, at r squared.
visual: pi r^2 h = 48pi peels apart, the 16 appears as a square of area 16 on the cylinder's base, and its side, 4, lights up in blue.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. r squared is not r. Take the root.

title: Volumes 8 and 27. The surface ratio is not 8 to 27
hook: Two similar solids have volumes 8 and 27. Ratio of their surface areas?
insight: Go back to length first: the cube root gives 2:3. Then square it for area: 4:9.
visual: Blocks of 8 and 27 collapse into edges of 2 and 3, then each edge sweeps out a face of 4 and 9 squares.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. From volume to area, pass through length.

title: SAT Area and Volume in 60 seconds
hook: Every SAT area and volume question is one of five pictures.
insight: Area is rectangles cut and moved: parallelograms, triangles as halves, circles as pi r^2. Volume is base x height, or one third of it for pointed solids, and scaling multiplies area by k^2 and volume by k^3.
visual: One rectangle shears into a parallelogram, halves into a triangle, rolls into a circle, extrudes into a prism, collapses into a pyramid and doubles into 8 copies, ending on a five-chip recap of cut, halve, stack, third, scale.
payoff: The whole Area and volume skill
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Every area and volume rule in one minute.

title: Parallel lines: these two angles are not equal
hook: Same-side interior angles: 3x + 10 and 5x - 30. Find x.
insight: Same-side interior angles add to 180, so 8x - 20 = 180, x = 25, and the angles are 85 and 95. Setting them equal gives x = 20 and two 70s, which breaks the picture.
visual: The equation 3x + 10 = 5x - 30 is inked and struck, then one angle slides along the transversal to sit beside the other on a straight line, filling 180.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. This parallel-lines trap is nearly certain.

title: Eight angles, only two sizes
hook: A line crosses two parallel lines. Eight angles. How many different sizes?
insight: Two. The lower crossing is an exact copy of the upper one slid along the transversal, so every angle is either a or 180 - a.
visual: The top crossing slides down the transversal and lands exactly on the bottom one, then all eight angles split into small ones in blue and large ones in ink.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Eight angles, two sizes. That is the whole topic.

title: An isosceles triangle with a 40 degree angle has two answers
hook: An isosceles triangle has a 40 degree angle. What could the largest angle be?
insight: Two cases: if 40 is the top angle, the others are 70 and 70; if 40 is a base angle, the angles are 40, 40 and 100. Could be means test both.
visual: The 40 degree mark jumps from the apex to a base corner and the triangle reshapes from tall and narrow to wide and flat, each version labeled.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Could-be questions often have two answers.

title: Similar triangles: use the whole side, not the piece
hook: DE parallel to BC. AD is 4, DB is 6, DE is 5. BC?
insight: Compare with the whole side AB = 4 + 6 = 10, not the piece DB: BC = 5 x 10 / 4 = 12.5. Using 6 / 4 gives 7.5.
visual: The setup 5 x 6 / 4 is struck, then the small triangle ADE scales up from vertex A until it fills ABC, with the ratio 10/4 on a chip.
payoff: Similar triangles with a parallel segment
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Use the whole side, never just the piece.

title: Why side-side-angle does not prove congruence
hook: Two sides and an angle that isn't between them. Same triangle every time?
insight: No. With a 30 degree angle, an adjacent side of 8 and an opposite side of 5, the 5 can swing to hit the base line in two places, making two different triangles.
visual: A side of length 5 swings like a pendulum from the top vertex and touches the base line at two points, drawing two different triangles in turn.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. SSA swings two ways. That is why it fails.

title: Parallel lines to polygons: SAT angles in 60 seconds
hook: Every angle fact the SAT tests fits on one page.
insight: A straight line is 180, vertical angles match, and parallel lines make only two sizes, a and 180 - a. A triangle is 180, its exterior angle is the two far angles combined, and an n-gon is (n - 2) x 180.
visual: One line gets crossed, copied in parallel, closed into a triangle and extended into a pentagon, each step adding a chip to a recap of line, cross, parallel, triangle, polygon.
payoff: The whole Lines, angles, and triangles skill
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Every angle rule in one minute.

title: sin A is not 5/13 here
hook: Right angle at C, AC 5, BC 12, AB 13. What is sin A?
insight: Stand at A: the side across from A is BC = 12, so sin A = 12/13. 5/13 is cos A.
visual: An eye sits at vertex A, a sight line crosses the triangle and lights BC in blue as opposite, and the answer 5/13 is struck.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Label opposite and adjacent from the named angle.

title: Why sin 30 equals cos 60
hook: Why does sin 30 equal cos 60?
insight: The two acute angles of a right triangle add to 90, and the side opposite one is adjacent to the other. So the sine of an angle is the cosine of its complement: sin x = cos(90 - x).
visual: One right triangle stays still while the viewpoint jumps from the 30 degree corner to the 60 degree corner, and the labels opposite and adjacent swap places on the same blue side.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Sine and cosine swap. Here is the whole reason.

title: A 45-45-90 with hypotenuse 10 has area 25, not 50
hook: A right isosceles triangle has hypotenuse 10. What is its area?
insight: The legs are 10/sqrt2 = 5sqrt2, so the area is 1/2 x 5sqrt2 x 5sqrt2 = 25. Faster: four of these triangles tile a 10 by 10 square, so each is 100 / 4.
visual: Four copies of the triangle rotate around one point and tile a 10 by 10 square, the area chip dividing 100 by 4 while 50 is struck.
urgent_hook: Scores are out. Special triangles from area cost 750s. Fix it before {test}.

title: SAT Trig in 60 seconds: one triangle, five views
hook: All of SAT trig is one right triangle seen five ways.
insight: Sine, cosine and tangent are side ratios fixed by the angle because similar triangles share them, and the acute angles swap roles, so sin x = cos(90 - x). Special triangles are half a square and half an equilateral, and radians measure angles in radius lengths.
visual: One right triangle carries through: it labels its sides, scales without changing ratios, swaps viewpoint corners, splits from a square and an equilateral, then sits in a circle as its radius wraps the arc, ending on a five-chip recap.
payoff: The whole Right triangles and trigonometry skill
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. All of SAT trig in one minute.

title: The 5 SAT geometry questions behind most hard misses
hook: These five geometry questions live in the hard module.
insight: Special triangles from an area, sin x = cos y with algebra, a circle that needs completing the square, volume scaled by k^3, and slant height inside a pyramid. Each falls to one move: halve, add to 90, complete both squares, cube the ratio, find the hidden right triangle.
visual: Five figures slide in one per beat and each solves in a single motion, ending on a recap row of halves, complements, squares, cubes and slants.
urgent_hook: Scores are out. If geometry cost you, these five patterns are your plan for {test}.

title: What a radian actually is
hook: Why is 180 degrees the same as pi radians?
insight: A radian is the angle you get by bending one radius onto the circle, about 57.3 degrees. Half a circle takes pi radius lengths, so pi radians = 180 degrees.
visual: A radius peels off and wraps along the rim, copies laying down end to end, 1, 2, 3 and a bit, stopping at the halfway point with pi in blue.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. A radian is a radius bent onto the circle.

title: The center of this circle is not (3, -2)
hook: (x + 3)^2 + (y - 2)^2 = 16. Center and radius?
insight: The form is (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2, so x + 3 means h = -3 and the center is (-3, 2). The 16 is r^2, so the radius is 4, not 16.
visual: x + 3 rewrites itself as x - (-3), the center dot slides to (-3, 2), and a radius of 4 sweeps out the circle while 16 is struck.
payoff: Center and radius from a circle equation
urgent_hook: {test} is in {days} days. Flip the center's signs. Root the right side.

title: SAT Geometry and Trig in 60 seconds
hook: SAT geometry is one triangle doing four jobs.
insight: Parallel lines give only two angles, and similar triangles scale lengths by k and areas by k^2. Trig ratios are fixed by the angle with sin x = cos(90 - x), and a circle is Pythagoras spun around a center.
visual: One triangle is cut by parallel lines, scales up with its area tiling by k^2, gets its sides labeled with trig ratios, then spins inside a circle, ending on a recap of angles, scaling, ratios, circles.
payoff: The whole Geometry and Trigonometry domain
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. All of SAT geometry in one minute.

title: SAT Data Analysis in 60 seconds: percents to margin of error
hook: Five to seven SAT questions. Five pictures. Here they are.
insight: Beats: a percent change is a multiplier (up 20% is x1.2), the mean is a balance point while the median just counts to the middle, 'given' shrinks a two-way table to one row, a best-fit line predicts and a residual is actual minus predicted, and a margin of error is a range for the population, not for individuals.
visual: One data set carries the whole video: a bar stretches by x1.2, the same dots sit on a seesaw with a median flag, a two-way table fades to a single row, the dots become a scatterplot with residual sticks, then a +/- bracket forms around an estimate.
payoff: every Problem-Solving and Data Analysis question type
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. These five data pictures cover 5 to 7 questions.

title: One-variable linear equations: the whole SAT skill in 60 seconds
hook: Every one-variable equation on the SAT needs one of four moves.
insight: Beats: clear fractions by multiplying every term by the common denominator, distribute a negative to every term, look for the asked expression (like 2x + 3) already grouped inside, and if x cancels, a false statement means no solution and a true one means infinitely many, while different x-coefficients always give exactly one solution.
visual: A balance holds 3x/4 - 1/2 = x/2 + 1; every term multiplies by 4 in one sweep, a minus sign sprays onto each term in a parenthesis, a 2x + 3 block lights inside an equation, then both sides become lines that cross, run parallel, or merge.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Every one-variable equation on it needs one of these moves.

title: Linear functions on the SAT in 60 seconds
hook: A gym charges $40 to join and $25 a month. That's the skill.
insight: Beats: f(x) = 25x + 40, where 40 is the value at x = 0 and 25 is the change per month; slope from two points is change in y over change in x; raising x by 3 raises f by 3 x 25 = 75; f(3) means plug in (115) while f(x) = 140 means solve (x = 4); and 'first month A, each additional B' is A + B(x - 1).
visual: A staircase of identical $25 steps climbs from a $40 starting dot, a slope triangle slides along the line, a vertical probe reads f(3) = 115, and a horizontal probe at 140 finds x = 4.
payoff: Linear functions: slope, intercept, f(k), models
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Expect about four linear-function questions; here is every type.

title: 2x + 3y = 12: two-variable lines in 60 seconds
hook: 2x + 3y = 12. Five SAT question types live inside this line.
insight: Beats: the slope is -A/B = -2/3; the intercepts come from zeroing the other variable (x = 6, y = 4); a point lies on the line exactly when it makes the equation true; the coefficients are per-item prices in a two-item total; and a parallel line keeps -2/3 while a perpendicular one takes 3/2.
visual: The line 2x + 3y = 12 draws between (6, 0) and (0, 4), a slope triangle reads -2/3, a test point drops onto it and checks, price tags $2 and $3 slide onto x and y, then a twin parallel line and a quarter-turned perpendicular line appear.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. One line, five question types, sixty seconds.

title: Nonlinear equations and systems in 60 seconds
hook: A line meets a parabola. How many times? Every answer is here.
insight: Beats: solve a quadratic by factoring or the formula; the discriminant b^2 - 4ac says 2, 1 or 0 real solutions; substitute a line into a parabola to get one quadratic; squaring both sides can add a fake root, so check each one; and |x - 3| = 5 has two answers, 8 and -2.
visual: A line sweeps down across a parabola as a counter reads 2, then 1 at the kiss, then 0; a square-root curve and a line meet once while a ghost mirror branch adds a fake second crossing that fades; a ruler swings 5 each way from 3.
payoff: Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems in two variables
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. These hard-module questions all reduce to counting crossings.

title: One-variable data in 60 seconds: mean, median, spread
hook: Mean, median, spread, outliers. Four questions, one dot plot.
insight: Beats: the mean is the balance point, total over count weighted by frequency; the median is the value at position (n + 1)/2; removing an outlier drags the mean but barely moves the median; standard deviation is typical distance from the mean, unchanged when every value shifts; and a combined mean is total over total, not an average of averages.
visual: A dot plot sits on a seesaw: the fulcrum finds the mean, a flag counts to the middle dot, an outlier slides away dragging the fulcrum while the flag stays, distance sticks show spread, then the whole plot shifts right with the sticks unchanged.
payoff: One-variable data: distributions and measures of center and spread
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Every mean and median question is this one seesaw.

title: Lines, angles and triangles in 60 seconds
hook: Eight angles at a transversal. How many different sizes? Two.
insight: Beats: parallel lines cut by a transversal make only two angles, a and 180 - a; a triangle's corners tear off into a straight 180; an exterior angle equals the two far interior angles; a segment parallel to a side cuts off a similar triangle with every side scaled by k; and a polygon's angles add to (n - 2) x 180.
visual: A transversal colors its eight angles into two groups, a triangle's corners rip off and line up flat, a parallel segment slides inside a triangle to make a smaller similar copy, then a hexagon fans into four triangles.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Angle questions only ever use these five facts.

title: Trig in 60 seconds: the parts the SAT actually uses
hook: Trigonometry, the whole class. The SAT needs five ideas from it.
insight: Beats: sine and cosine are the height and width of a point turning on a circle of radius 1, which in a right triangle become opposite/hypotenuse and adjacent/hypotenuse; tangent is the slope of the radius; sin x = cos(90 - x) because the acute angles swap sides; special triangles give exact values like sin 30 = 1/2; and radians measure angles in radius lengths, pi = 180 degrees.
visual: Nav 'Alg 1 · Alg 2 · Geo · Trig' with Trig underlined; a point turns on a unit circle dropping a right triangle whose legs read cos and sin, the radius's slope labels tan, the triangle flips across y = x to swap sin and cos, and a radius bends around the rim to show one radian.
payoff: trig and radian questions, mapped to the class you took
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Here is all the trig it asks, in five ideas.

title: The SAT reference sheet in 60 seconds, every formula explained
hook: The SAT gives you 12 formulas and 3 facts. Here's why each is true.
insight: Beats: circle area and circumference, rectangle area, and the triangle as half a rectangle; Pythagoras plus the two special triangles, half a square and half an equilateral; box and cylinder as base times height; cone and pyramid as one third of their box, and the sphere as 4/3 pi r^3; and the facts 360 degrees = 2 pi radians and triangle angles sum to 180.
visual: The reference sheet fills the page, then each icon lifts off in turn and does its one move: a rectangle halves into a triangle, a square and an equilateral triangle split, a base sweeps up into a prism, and three pyramids fill a cube.
payoff: geometry questions where the formula is given to you
urgent_hook: {test} is in {days} days. Know this sheet cold so you never stop to open it.

title: Every 'how many solutions' SAT question in 60 seconds
hook: Zero, one, two, or infinitely many. Count the crossings.
insight: Beats: a linear equation has one solution unless x cancels (false leaves none, true leaves infinitely many); a linear system has none when the lines are parallel and infinitely many when they coincide; a quadratic has 2, 1 or 0 by the sign of b^2 - 4ac; a line meets a parabola 0, 1 or 2 times; and 'exactly one' is always the tangent case.
visual: One grid hosts every case: two lines crossing, turning parallel, merging; then a parabola rising through the axis with a counter 2-1-0; then a line sliding down to graze a parabola at exactly one point.
payoff: number-of-solutions questions in Algebra and Advanced Math
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Every 'how many solutions' question, decided by counting crossings.

title: You solved for x. The SAT asked for 2x - 3.
hook: If 4x - 6 = 18, what is 2x - 3?
insight: 9: halve both sides and 2x - 3 = 9 appears directly. Solving gives x = 6, the most common wrong answer, and it is waiting in the choices.
visual: The equation 4x - 6 = 18 sits on a balance; the tempting x = 6 is inked then struck in blue, then the whole balance shrinks by half in one smooth scale to 2x - 3 = 9, the answer in accent.
payoff: 'find the value of the expression' questions
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Read the last line twice; this trap is on every test.

title: You found 180. The SAT asked for hours.
hook: A pump moves 3 gallons per minute. How many hours for 540 gallons?
insight: 540/3 = 180 is minutes, and 180 sits in the choices as bait; divide by 60 to get 3 hours. Circle the unit in the question before you compute.
visual: 540 gallons drain into 3-gallon buckets as a mono counter climbs to '180 min', the 180 is struck in blue, and a clock face sweeps three full turns to land on 3 hours in accent.
urgent_hook: It's {test} today. Before you bubble a number, check its unit.

title: 130 students, 40 per bus. The answer is not 3.25.
hook: 130 students, 40 seats per bus. How many buses?
insight: 4: 130/40 = 3.25, but a quarter bus doesn't exist, so the story forces rounding up. Had it asked how many buses can be completely filled, the answer would round down to 3; the context decides the direction.
visual: Students fill bus outlines 40 at a time; three buses fill, ten students stand outside, a fourth bus slides in for them in accent, and 3.25 is struck beside the answer 4.
payoff: whole-number answers from inequalities and rates
urgent_hook: It's {test} today. Before you round, ask what the story allows.

title: What separates a 700 from a 750 in SAT math
hook: Scores are out. Above 700, five question patterns make the difference.
insight: In the hardest band of the official question bank, five patterns recur: a discriminant with a parameter (17 items), percents of 100% or more (16), no-solution systems with a constant k (12), a line tangent to a parabola, and k^2 and k^3 scaling (56% hard). Master those five and the hard module has few surprises left.
visual: Five mini diagrams build in sequence under the nav 'disc · percent · no-sol · tangent · scale': a parabola touching the axis, a bar growing to five copies, two parallel lines, a line grazing a curve, and a square tiling into four.
payoff: the hard-module questions that decide top scores
urgent_hook: Scores for {test} are out. These five patterns separate 700 from 750.

title: 1 inch = 3 miles. 2 square inches is not 6 square miles.
hook: 1 inch = 3 miles. A park is 2 square inches. Real area?
insight: 18 square miles: one square inch stands for a 3-by-3 mile square, which is 9 square miles, so 2 x 9 = 18. Lengths scale by k, areas by k^2 and volumes by k^3, the same rule behind similar figures and square-unit conversions like 1 yd^2 = 9 ft^2.
visual: A 1-inch map square stretches into a 3-mile square that tiles into a 3 by 3 grid of one-mile squares, the struck answer 6 sits beside 18 in accent, then a cube stretches into a 3 by 3 by 3 block of 27.
urgent_hook: Retaking {test}? This k-squared trap hides in three different hard-module topics.

title: Why hard SAT questions replace numbers with k
hook: Hard SAT questions swap a number for k. What does k really ask?
insight: A constant like k turns one graph into a whole family, and the question asks for the member where something special happens: two lines go parallel, a line just touches a curve, or a value hits a boundary. Picture the family moving and look for that moment.
visual: A line labeled kx sweeps through a fan of positions, a parabola labeled + k rises through a stack of copies, and in each family one member flashes in accent at the special moment: parallel, then tangent.
payoff: parameter questions in Algebra and Advanced Math
urgent_hook: Retaking on {date}? Every hard 'find k' question is the same idea.

title: Midpoint, vertex, circle center, mean: one average
hook: The zeros are 2 and 8. Where is the vertex?
insight: At x = 5, the average (2 + 8)/2: a parabola's vertex sits midway between its zeros, a segment's midpoint averages its endpoints, a circle's center is the midpoint of any diameter, and the mean is the balance point of data.
visual: Two dots at 2 and 8 stay fixed while four pictures form around them in turn: a segment with its midpoint, a parabola folding at x = 5, a circle on that diameter, and a seesaw balancing at 5.
payoff: vertex, midpoint, circle-center and mean questions
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Four formulas you can replace with one average.

title: Parallel lines run three SAT topics at once
hook: Same slope, same angles, same shape. One idea, three topics.
insight: Parallel lines never meet, so a system with equal slopes has no solution; a transversal cuts them at only two angle sizes; and a line parallel to a triangle's side cuts off a smaller similar triangle. One property, three question types.
visual: Two parallel lines on a grid show their crossing point running off to infinity, a transversal colors eight angles into two groups, then the lines tilt into a triangle's base and a parallel cut, the small triangle scaling into the big one.
payoff: no-solution systems, angle chasing and similar triangles
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Learn parallel lines once, use them three ways.

title: One function, four disguises: story, table, graph, equation
hook: A plant is 4 cm tall and grows 2 cm a week. Four ways.
insight: The story, the table (0, 4), (1, 6), (2, 8), the line through those points and h = 2w + 4 are one object. Matching questions only ask you to translate, so test two clear points from one form in the other.
visual: A sentence card folds into a table, the table's rows lift off as dots onto a grid, the dots join into a line, and the line's rise and intercept write h = 2w + 4.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Every matching question is the same function in disguise.

title: Count the gridlines and you'll get the slope wrong
hook: The line rises 3 gridlines for every 2 across. Is the slope 3/2?
insight: Not here: the y gridlines are every 10 and the x gridlines every 5, so the rise is 30 and the run is 10, and the slope is 3. Read two labeled points, never the boxes.
visual: A slope triangle spans 3 boxes up and 2 across with 3/2 inked then struck in blue, the axis labels 10, 20, 30 and 5, 10 brighten, and the triangle's legs relabel to 30 and 10.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Check the axis scale before you count anything.

title: Is sqrt(9) + sqrt(16) equal to sqrt(25)?
hook: sqrt(9) + sqrt(16). Is that the same as sqrt(25)?
insight: No: 3 + 4 = 7, but sqrt 25 = 5. Picture a right triangle with legs 3 and 4: walking both legs is 7, the hypotenuse is 5, and the shortcut is always shorter, so sqrt(a + b) < sqrt(a) + sqrt(b) for positive a and b.
visual: A right triangle with legs 3 and 4 draws; a dot walks both legs while a counter reaches 7, then walks the hypotenuse and stops at 5, and the equation sqrt 9 + sqrt 16 = sqrt 25 is struck in blue.
payoff: radical expressions and the Pythagorean theorem
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Roots don't add; one triangle shows why.

title: Delete every fraction from an equation in one move
hook: x/3 + x/4 = 7. Make the fractions disappear first.
insight: Multiply every term, including the 7, by 12: 4x + 3x = 84, so 7x = 84 and x = 12. Check: 12/3 + 12/4 = 4 + 3 = 7.
visual: A x12 stamp presses on every term of the balance at once and the denominators drop away, leaving 4x + 3x = 84 in ink.
urgent_hook: {test} is on {date}. Clear fractions this way and bank a minute.

skill: Systems of two linear equations in two variables
title: 30 heads, 74 legs. How many cows? No algebra
hook: Chickens and cows: 30 heads, 74 legs. How many cows?
insight: Pretend all 30 are chickens: 60 legs. The extra 14 legs come from cows, 2 extra each, so 7 cows and 23 chickens.
visual: Thirty birds stand in a row with 60 legs counted, then 7 of them sprout two extra legs one by one as the counter climbs to 74.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Pretend they're all one kind, then fix it.

title: Three triangles, one base. Which one is biggest?
hook: Base 6, tips on a line 4 above it. Which triangle is biggest?
insight: None of them: all three have area 1/2 x 6 x 4 = 12. Area depends on the base and the perpendicular height, not on how far the triangle leans.
visual: One tip slides along a dashed line parallel to the base, the triangle leaning further and further, while the area chip stays frozen at 12.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Height decides a triangle's area, not its lean.

title: One 18-inch pizza or two 12-inch pizzas?
hook: One 18-inch pizza or two 12-inch pizzas. Which is more pizza?
insight: The single 18-inch: 81pi, about 254 square inches, against 2 x 36pi = 72pi, about 226. Area grows with the square of the width, so 1.5 times wider is 2.25 times the pizza.
visual: Two 12-inch circles are cut into wedges and laid over the 18-inch circle, and a blue crescent of uncovered pizza is left showing.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Area grows with the square. This pizza proves it.

title: What you can stop studying for SAT math
hook: Logarithms, matrices, complex numbers. Stop studying them for the SAT.
insight: Across the 1,925 math items in the official question bank, logarithms, matrices, complex numbers, sequences, function composition and the remainder theorem barely appear. Spend that time by the real domain weights: about 35% Algebra, 35% Advanced Math, 15% Data, 15% Geometry and Trig.
visual: Topic cards for logarithms, matrices and complex numbers fade to label gray and slide off the page, then one bar splits 35-35-15-15 and fills with the four domain names.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Here is what you can stop studying tonight.

title: 1,925 official SAT math questions, about 150 patterns
hook: The official bank has 1,925 math questions. How many ideas are there?
insight: Sorted by what they actually ask, the bank's 1,925 math items fall into about 150 recurring patterns, like 'expand a polynomial' (about 63), 'a point lies on the line' (48) and 'percent of a quantity' (about 46). The same pattern returns with new numbers, so practicing patterns beats random drilling.
visual: 1,925 tiny dots scatter across the page, then drift into labeled piles that sort themselves by size, the three biggest piles outlined in accent with mono counts 63, 48 and 46.
payoff: study planning from the official question bank
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Study the patterns that repeat, not random questions.

title: Two questions in each SAT module don't count. You can't tell which.
hook: Stuck on a strange question? It might not even count.
insight: Each math module has 22 questions, but 2 are unscored pretest items mixed in invisibly, so 20 count. One weird question is never worth five minutes: answer your best guess, flag it, and move on; College Board says guessing beats leaving a blank.
visual: A row of 22 question tiles draws across the page, two of them flicker faintly and fade to label gray while a mono counter reads '20 scored', then a stuck clock hand releases and moves on.
urgent_hook: It's {test} today. If one question feels strange, guess, flag it, and move on.

title: kx + 3 = 4x - 7 has no solution. Find k in two seconds
hook: kx + 3 = 4x - 7 has no solution. What is k?
insight: No solution means x must cancel and leave a false statement: k = 4 turns it into 3 = -7, which is never true. Moving 4x across and answering k = -4 is the sign trap.
visual: Graph y = kx + 3 and y = 4x - 7; a blue slider turns k and the crossing point races off the page exactly as the lines go parallel at k = 4.
payoff: "for what k is there no solution" equations
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. No solution means same slope. That's the whole trick.

title: One has no solution, one has infinitely many. Which is which?
hook: 2(x+3) = 2x+6 or 2x+5: which has no solution?
insight: Expand: 2x + 6 = 2x + 6 is true for every x (same line, infinitely many), while 2x + 6 = 2x + 5 is never true (parallel lines, no solution). The tempting move is to swap them.
visual: The left side expands into 2x + 6, then two right-side lines appear: one slides exactly onto it and merges, the other stays one unit below, parallel forever.
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Don't swap these two endings on it.

title: Why 0 = 0 means every number is a solution
hook: You solved an equation and got 0 = 0. What does that mean?
insight: Once the x's cancel, what's left no longer depends on x, so it is equally true or false for every x. A true leftover like 0 = 0 means every x works; a false one like 0 = 5 means none does.
visual: A dial spins x through -3, 0, 2 and 10 while both sides of 4x + 1 = 4x + 1 move in lockstep with a gap readout stuck at 0, then the right side becomes 4x + 6 and the gap freezes at 5.
urgent_hook: {test} is in {days} days. Know what 0 = 0 means before you sit down.

title: The 7s cancel, so no solution? Wrong. It's x = 0
hook: 3x + 7 = 5x + 7. How many solutions?
insight: Different x-coefficients always give exactly one solution. Here 3x = 5x forces x = 0, which is a real solution, not "no solution".
visual: The two 7s cancel and fade, the words no solution appear and are struck in blue, and the graphs y = 3x + 7 and y = 5x + 7 cross right at (0, 7).
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Zero is a solution. Don't throw it away.

title: Every no-solution question is secretly dividing by zero
hook: ax + b = cx + d. What happens when a equals c?
insight: Solving gives x = (d - b)/(a - c). When a = c you would divide by zero: if d = b too it is 0/0 and every x works, otherwise it is a nonzero number over 0 and no x works.
visual: The general solution x = (d - b)/(a - c) builds step by step, then a slider pushes a toward c, the denominator shrinks to 0 in mono, and the answer dot slides off the end of the number line.
