title: Why a can's label is 2 pi r h
hook: Peel the label off a can. What shape is it?
insight: A rectangle: its height is the can's height and its width is the circumference, 2pi r. A can of radius 3 and height 10 has a label of 2pi x 3 x 10 = 60pi.
visual: The label peels away from a wireframe cylinder and unrolls flat into a rectangle whose sides read h and 2pi r.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. A cylinder's side is just a rectangle.

title: Angles in ratio 1:2:3:4. The largest is not 72
hook: A quadrilateral's angles are in the ratio 1:2:3:4. Largest angle?
insight: A quadrilateral's angles add to 360, not 180: 10 parts of 36, so the largest is 4 x 36 = 144. Using 180 gives 72.
visual: A diagonal splits the quadrilateral into two triangles, 180 + 180, then a 360 bar divides into 10 equal blocks and four of them glow blue.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Four sides means 360. Then split the ratio.

title: Why a polygon's angles add to (n - 2) x 180
hook: Why does a pentagon's angle sum equal 540?
insight: Diagonals from one corner split any n-sided polygon into n - 2 triangles of 180 each. A pentagon is 3 triangles, 540, and a hexagon is 4, 720.
visual: Diagonals fan out from one corner of a pentagon, three triangles light up in turn, and the counter climbs 180, 360, 540.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Count the triangles, not the sides.

title: Why sine only depends on the angle
hook: DEF is triangle ABC tripled. If sin A is 0.6, what is sin D?
insight: Still 0.6. Scaling multiplies the opposite side and the hypotenuse by the same factor, so their ratio cannot change: sine is a ratio fixed by the angle alone.
visual: A 3-4-5 right triangle scales up to 9-12-15 and down to 1.5-2-2.5 while the ratio readout stays locked at 0.6.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Similar triangles share every trig ratio.

title: The point (k, 3) is on this circle. k has two values
hook: (k, 3) is on x^2 + y^2 = 25. What could k be?
insight: 4 or -4: k^2 + 9 = 25, so k^2 = 16. A horizontal line at height 3 crosses the circle twice.
visual: A horizontal dashed line at y = 3 slides across the circle and two dots appear at x = -4 and x = 4, the second one turning blue.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. A square root has two signs. So does k.

title: Shift a circle and the radius stays put
hook: Shift (x-2)^2 + (y+1)^2 = 9 right 3, then double its radius.
insight: Shifting moves only the center, to (5, -1). Doubling the radius from 3 to 6 multiplies the right side by 4: (x - 5)^2 + (y + 1)^2 = 36, not 18.
visual: The circle glides 3 units right as a rigid ring, then expands from its center while the right side ticks from 9 to 36 and 18 is struck.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Shifts move the center. Only scaling changes r.

title: Why a tangent line meets the radius at 90 degrees
hook: Where a line just touches a circle, why is the angle exactly 90?
insight: The touching point is the closest point on the line to the center, because every other point on the line is outside the circle. The shortest path to a line is perpendicular, so the radius meets the tangent at 90 degrees.
visual: A line slides toward a circle until it touches, dashed segments from the center to other points on the line all overshoot the rim, and the shortest one, the radius, locks at a right angle.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Tangent and radius always meet at 90.

title: The tangent's slope is not the radius's slope
hook: Circle x^2 + y^2 = 25. Slope of the tangent line at (3, 4)?
insight: The radius to (3, 4) has slope 4/3, and the tangent is perpendicular to it, so its slope is the negative reciprocal, -3/4.
visual: The radius from the origin to (3, 4) draws with slope 4/3 and is struck as an answer, then a line through (3, 4) rotates until it meets the radius at 90 and reads -3/4.
urgent_hook: Retaking on {date}? Tangent lines are perpendicular slopes in disguise.

title: Tangent length is not 13 minus 5
hook: A point 13 from the center of a radius-5 circle. Tangent length?
insight: The tangent is 12, because the radius meets it at 90 degrees and forms a 5-12-13 right triangle with the center and the outside point. 13 - 5 = 8 measures the gap to the rim instead.
visual: Two tangent lines sweep from the outside point to the circle, a radius drops in at a right angle, and the 5-12-13 triangle lights up while 8 is struck.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. A tangent always builds a right triangle.

title: A chord of 8 in a circle of radius 5
hook: A chord of 8 in a circle of radius 5. Distance from center?
insight: The distance is 3: the perpendicular from the center cuts the chord in half, so the radius 5 is the hypotenuse over a half-chord of 4, a 3-4-5 triangle. Using the whole 8 as a leg fails.
visual: A perpendicular drops from the center onto the chord and splits it into 4 and 4, a radius swings to the chord's end, and the 3-4-5 triangle lights up.
payoff: Chords and right triangles in circles
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Halve the chord and Pythagoras finishes it.

title: Which conclusion is allowed? SAT study design in 60 seconds
hook: Can this study say coffee causes better grades?
insight: Beats: random sampling lets you generalize to the population that was sampled; random assignment to groups lets you claim cause; an observational study with neither shows only an association; and results never stretch beyond the group that was actually sampled.
visual: A 2x2 grid labeled 'randomly sampled' and 'randomly assigned' fills one cell at a time, each cell stamping the claim it allows, while a population circle shrinks to just the sampled group.
payoff: Evaluating statistical claims: observational studies and experiments
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. One 2x2 grid answers every study-design question.

title: 10 SAT math question types you will very likely see
hook: Ten question types that show up on nearly every SAT. Ready?
insight: Mathchops' tagging of the official adaptive practice tests ranks these ten most common: interpret a y-intercept, interpret a slope, solve a 2x2 system, evaluate a function, interpret an exponential model, percent of a quantity, the slope of Ax + By = C, intercepts and zeros, factoring, and expanding a polynomial.
visual: A 10-cell grid fills one cell per second, each cell drawing its signature picture in ink, with a mono counter 01/10 to 10/10 and the most frequent cells outlined in accent.
payoff: the highest-frequency patterns across all four domains
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. These ten are the most common question types on it.

title: Your answer is 2/3. Type 0.67 and it's marked wrong.
hook: Your answer is 2/3. Is 0.67 accepted?
insight: No. A decimal too long for the box must be truncated or rounded at the fourth digit, so .6666, .6667, 0.666 and 0.667 are fine and 2/3 itself is safest. A positive answer gets 5 characters and a negative one gets 6, counting the minus sign.
visual: Five empty character slots draw in a row; 0.67 drops in leaving a gap and is struck in blue, then .6667 fills every slot, and a sixth slot appears only when a minus sign arrives.
urgent_hook: {test} is in {days} days. Learn the 5-character rule before you see the box.

title: The SAT asks for a percent. Do you type 40%, 40 or 0.4?
hook: The answer is 40%. What exactly do you type?
insight: Type 40 when the question asks for the percent or for p in p%; the directions forbid percent signs, dollar signs and commas. Read what the blank stands for: 'as a decimal' wants 0.4, and $1,200 goes in as 1200.
visual: An entry box receives 40%, the % sign lifts off and is struck in blue, a $1,200 entry sheds its $ and comma into 1200, and a label 'p% = 40%' points p at 40 in accent.
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Strip the percent sign; here is exactly what to enter.

title: Why a number is divisible by 9 when its digits are
hook: Is 738 divisible by 9? Add the digits.
insight: 7 + 3 + 8 = 18, so yes: 738 = 82 x 9. Every 10 is 9 plus 1 and every 100 is 99 plus 1, so 738 is a multiple of 9 plus 7 + 3 + 8, which leaves just the digit sum to check.
visual: 738 splits into 7 hundred-blocks, 3 ten-rods and 8 ones; each hundred sheds a 99 chunk and each ten sheds a 9 chunk into a gray pile of nines, leaving 7 + 3 + 8 = 18 loose ones.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Check arithmetic in two seconds with this rule.

title: x/5 = 3. What is 5/x? It isn't 15
hook: If x/5 = 3, what is 5/x?
insight: Flip both sides: if x/5 = 3, then 5/x = 1/3. You never need x = 15, which is the trap choice.
visual: The fraction x/5 rotates a half turn on its bar into 5/x while the 3 beside it flips into 1/3.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days out. Flip it, don't solve it.

title: a(x - 2) + 7 = 5x + b for every x. What is a + b?
hook: a(x-2)+7 = 5x+b has infinitely many solutions. Find a+b.
insight: Infinitely many means both sides are the same line: match the x-terms (a = 5) and the constants (-2a + 7 = b, so b = -3). So a + b = 2.
visual: The left side expands to ax - 2a + 7, and its pieces slide under the right side's 5x and b like matching tiles, filling in a = 5 and b = -3.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Match both parts, not just the x's.

title: Kill three answer choices with two glances
hook: Four graphs, one equation: which graph is y = -2x + 3?
insight: First glance: the y-intercept must be 3, which removes most choices. Second glance: the line must fall from left to right because the slope is negative. Whatever survives is the answer.
visual: Four small graphs sit in a grid, two are struck in blue when their y-intercept isn't 3, then one more when it rises instead of falls.
urgent_hook: {test} is today. Two glances beat graphing every choice.

title: Is f(2x) the same as 2f(x)? One number says no
hook: f(x) = 3x + 2. Is f(2x) equal to 2f(x)?
insight: f(2x) feeds 2x in: 3(2x) + 2 = 6x + 2. 2f(x) doubles the output: 6x + 4. They differ by 2, because only the second doubles the +2.
visual: Two machines sit side by side, one doubling the input before it goes in and one doubling the output after it comes out, and the +2 tile visibly duplicates only in the second.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Watch where the 2 goes.

title: a < 0 and b > 0. Which quadrant does y = ax + b never touch?
hook: y = ax + b, a negative, b positive. Which quadrant is skipped?
insight: For any negative x, ax is positive, so y = ax + b is bigger than b, which is positive: the line never enters quadrant III.
visual: A line pinned at a positive intercept tilts through every negative slope like a clock hand, sweeping quadrants II, I and IV while quadrant III stays empty.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Reason with signs, not numbers.

title: Perpendicular to 2x + 5y = 10 in one move: swap and flip
hook: Write a line perpendicular to 2x + 5y = 10 without finding slopes.
insight: Swap A and B and flip one sign: 5x - 2y = D is perpendicular, since the slopes -2/5 and 5/2 multiply to -1. A parallel line keeps 2x + 5y and changes only the constant.
visual: The coefficients 2 and 5 trade places, a minus sign hops onto one of them, and the new line rotates a quarter turn about the crossing point into place.
payoff: perpendicular and parallel lines in standard form
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Swap and flip for any perpendicular line.

title: 5 more adult tickets means how many fewer kid tickets?
hook: 8a + 5c = 200. Buy 5 more adult tickets. How many fewer kids?
insight: 5 more adults cost 5 times 8 = $40, which is exactly 8 kid tickets at $5. So the exchange rate is 5 adults for 8 kids: the slope -8/5 in disguise.
visual: Five adult tokens drop onto a point on the budget line, which slides down and right as eight kid tokens leave, tracing a slope triangle 5 across and 8 down.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. The coefficients are the exchange rate.

title: The line y = 4x - 9 passes through (p, p). Find p
hook: y = 4x - 9 goes through the point (p, p). What is p?
insight: Equal coordinates means the point is on y = x, so p = 4p - 9, 3p = 9 and p = 3. Check: 4(3) - 9 = 3.
visual: The diagonal y = x draws in dashed gray, the line y = 4x - 9 crosses it, and the meeting dot lights up at (3, 3).
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Equal coordinates means y = x.

title: Pick the right equation with two dots on the grid
hook: This line hits (0, -2) and (3, 4). Which of four equations?
insight: Find two points where the line crosses grid corners exactly, then test each choice: (0, -2) and (3, 4) leave only y = 2x - 2. Two checks kill three choices.
visual: Two dots glow where the line crosses exact grid corners, then each answer choice is tested against them and three are struck in blue.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Two clean points beat any guess.

title: x + y = 10. How many solutions does it have?
hook: x + y = 10. How many solutions does it have?
insight: Infinitely many: (3, 7), (0, 10), (-2, 12) and (2.5, 7.5) all work, and together they form a whole line. A second equation is what pins down one point.
visual: Dots for (3, 7), (0, 10) and (-2, 12) appear one by one until they fuse into a solid line, then a second line crosses it and a single blue dot remains.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. One equation, two unknowns, a whole line.

skill: Systems of two linear equations in two variables
title: Find x + y without finding x or y
hook: 4x+7y=30 and 7x+4y=3. What is x + y?
insight: Mirrored coefficients mean you just add: 11x + 11y = 33, so x + y = 3. Solving fully gives x = -3 and y = 6, the long way to the same 3.
visual: The two equations slide together and add, the mirrored coefficients merge into 11x + 11y, and dividing by 11 drops 3 out in blue.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. If the coefficients mirror, just add.

skill: Systems of two linear equations in two variables
title: Find x^2 - y^2 from x + y = 9 and x - y = 5 without solving
hook: x+y = 9 and x-y = 5. What is x^2 - y^2?
insight: x^2 - y^2 factors as (x + y)(x - y) = 9 times 5 = 45, with no solving. Check: x = 7 and y = 2 give 49 - 4 = 45.
visual: A 7-by-7 square loses a 2-by-2 corner, and the L-shaped leftover slides into a 9-by-5 rectangle with area 45.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Factor first, solve never.

skill: Systems of two linear equations in two variables
title: 3x - 6y = 0. What is x/y? No solving needed
hook: If 3x - 6y = 0 and y is not 0, what is x/y?
insight: Move the y-term over: 3x = 6y. Divide both sides by 3y: x/y = 2. Pairs like (2, 1) and (10, 5) both work, so you can only find the ratio, never x itself.
visual: A line through the origin draws, dots at (2, 1), (4, 2) and (10, 5) light up along it, and each one's ratio chip reads 2.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Some questions only have a ratio. Find it fast.

skill: Systems of two linear equations in two variables
title: Infinitely many solutions. Find a/b without finding a or b
hook: ax+by=12 and 2x+8y=60 share infinitely many solutions. What is a/b?
insight: The same line means the same slope, so a/b = 2/8 = 1/4. The full values are a = 2/5 and b = 8/5, but the question never needed them.
visual: The two equations stack, the ratio a/b slides next to 2/8 as matching slope triangles, and 1/4 lights up while a and b stay blank.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Asked for a ratio? Find only the ratio.

skill: Linear inequalities in one or two variables
title: The elevator holds at most 2,000 lb. Is 28 boxes allowed?
hook: Elevator: at most 2,000 lb. Operator 180 lb, boxes 65 lb each. Max boxes?
insight: 180 + 65b <= 2000 gives b <= 28 exactly, and "at most" includes equality, so 28 boxes, landing exactly on 2,000 lb, is allowed. Answering 27 treats the limit as strict.
visual: Boxes load onto a scale whose needle creeps toward a 2,000 mark, the 28th box lands the needle exactly on the line, and a blue check appears.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. At most includes the limit itself.

skill: Linear inequalities in one or two variables
title: First hour $10, each extra hour $6, budget $50. Most hours?
hook: $10 for the first hour, $6 each additional, $50 budget. Most hours?
insight: 10 + 6(h - 1) <= 50 gives h - 1 <= 6.67, so at most 6 extra hours plus the first: 7 hours for $46. Eight hours would cost $52.
visual: The first $10 block sits under a $50 ceiling, $6 blocks stack on until the sixth fits at $46 and the seventh pokes through, then the counter adds the first hour back to read 7.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Count the extra units, then add the first back.

skill: Linear inequalities in one or two variables
title: Never flip an inequality sign again
hook: 5 - 4x < 21. Solve it without ever flipping the sign.
insight: Move the x-term to the side where it stays positive: 5 - 21 < 4x, so -16 < 4x and x > -4. Same answer as dividing by -4 and flipping, with nothing to forget.
visual: The -4x slides across the inequality and arrives as +4x on the right, the 21 slides left, and -4 < x reads off as x > -4.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Keep x positive and skip the flip.

skill: Linear inequalities in one or two variables
title: How many integers satisfy -5 < 2x + 3 <= 11?
hook: -5 < 2x + 3 <= 11. How many integers work?
insight: Do every step to all three parts: -8 < 2x <= 8, so -4 < x <= 4. That is -3 through 4: 8 integers, since -4 is excluded and 4 is included.
visual: The three-part inequality shrinks in place as -3 and /2 hit all three parts, then an open dot at -4 and a closed dot at 4 bracket eight blue ticks on the number line.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Open or closed endpoint? Count carefully.

title: Which is larger: 3^75 or 2^100? No calculator
hook: Which is larger, 3 to the 75th or 2 to the 100th?
insight: Both exponents share a factor of 25: 3^75 = (3^3)^25 = 27^25 and 2^100 = (2^4)^25 = 16^25. Same exponent, bigger base, so 3^75 is larger.
visual: Two long rows of 75 threes and 100 twos regroup into 25 bundles each, the bundles relabel as 27 and 16, and the 27 row rises above in accent blue.
payoff: Comparing powers by finding a common exponent
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Can you compare these two powers without a calculator?

skill: Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables
title: sqrt(6 + sqrt(6 + sqrt(6 + ...))) is exactly 3
hook: sqrt(6 + sqrt(6 + sqrt(6 + ...))), forever. What does it equal?
insight: The expression contains a copy of itself, so x = sqrt(6 + x), and squaring gives x^2 - x - 6 = 0, so x = 3 or -2. A square root can't be negative, so it is exactly 3.
visual: The infinite tower zooms out to reveal an identical tower nested inside, which gets boxed and renamed x, and the fake root -2 fades as 3 lands in accent.
payoff: Self-similar substitution and rejecting impossible roots
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Here's an infinite root with an exact answer.

title: 303^3 + 404^3 + 505^3 is a perfect cube
hook: What is 303 cubed plus 404 cubed plus 505 cubed?
insight: Each number is 101 times 3, 4 or 5, so factor out 101^3: 101^3(27 + 64 + 125) = 101^3 times 216 = 101^3 times 6^3 = 606^3.
visual: The three cubes shrink to 3^3, 4^3 and 5^3 as a common 101^3 slides out front, the small cubes stack into a 6-by-6-by-6 block, and 606^3 appears.
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Factor first, and giant numbers collapse.

title: 'Equivalent for all x'? Plug in x = 0 first
hook: x^2 + kx + 12 = (x + 3)(x + m). Find k.
insight: True for all x means true at x = 0, so 12 = 3m and m = 4. Then (x + 3)(x + 4) = x^2 + 7x + 12, so k = 7.
visual: A dial set to x = 0 fades every x-term to gray, leaving 12 = 3m, then the dial turns to x = 1 and confirms k = 7.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Identity question? Pick the easiest x and plug it in.

title: 9x^2 + kx + 16 is a perfect square. Find k
hook: 9x squared plus kx plus 16 is a perfect square. What's k?
insight: A perfect square (a + b)^2 has middle term 2ab, and here a = 3x and b = 4. So k = 2 times 3 times 4 = 24 (or -24), since (3x + 4)^2 = 9x^2 + 24x + 16.
visual: A 3x-by-3x square and a 4-by-4 square sit in opposite corners, two 3x-by-4 strips slide in to complete the big square, and their total 24x lights up.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Spot a perfect square from its middle term.

skill: Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables
title: Solve V = (1/3)pi r^2 h for r. Undo it backwards
hook: Solve V equals one-third pi r squared h for r.
insight: Undo the steps in reverse: multiply by 3, divide by pi h, then take the square root, so r = sqrt(3V/(pi h)). Forgetting the root, or dividing only one term, is the trap.
visual: The formula sits on a balance, 3, pi and h peel off one at a time to the other side, and a root sign closes over the result last.
payoff: Solving a formula for a variable
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Rearranging a formula shows up almost every test.

skill: Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables
title: |2x - 5| = 9. Find the sum of the solutions fast
hook: What is the sum of the solutions of |2x - 5| = 9?
insight: Solving 2x - 5 = 9 or -9 gives x = 7 or -2, which sum to 5. Faster: the solutions mirror each other around x = 5/2, where the inside is 0, so they sum to 2 times 5/2 = 5.
visual: A V-graph with its tip at x = 2.5 gets cut by the line y = 9 at -2 and 7, and equal arrows from the tip show the mirror symmetry.
payoff: Absolute value equations and sums of solutions
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Absolute value answers come in mirror pairs.

title: Lily pads double daily and cover the pond on day 30. Half?
hook: A pond's lily pads double daily. Full on day 30. Half full when?
insight: Day 29. Doubling means one step back halves it, so the pond is half covered just one day before it is full, not on day 15.
visual: A pond fills with blue tiles that double each day, the timeline rewinds one tick from day 30, and exactly half the pond empties.
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Exponential growth fools intuition. Test yours.

title: Two functions pass through (0, 4) and (1, 12). Are they the same?
hook: Two functions both pass through (0, 4) and (1, 12). Are they the same?
insight: Not necessarily: y = 8x + 4 adds 8 while y = 4 times 3^x triples, and both fit those two points. At x = 2 one gives 20 and the other 36, so you need the model type or a third point.
visual: A line and an exponential curve draw through the same two dots, then split apart past x = 1, landing at 20 and 36 with dashed guides.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Two points don't tell you the model type.

title: $100 a year or 8% a year on $1,000. Which wins?
hook: Start with $1,000. Add $100 a year, or grow 8% a year?
insight: The flat $100 leads for six years, but 8% compounds on a growing amount and by year 7 reaches about $1,714 against $1,700. After that it never looks back.
visual: A straight line and a gentle curve race from $1,000, the line leads at first, then the curve crosses it at year 7 and pulls away in blue.
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Linear versus exponential, settled by one race.

title: Vertex (2, -3), passes through (4, 5). Find the parabola
hook: A parabola has vertex 2, negative 3, and passes through 4, 5. Find a.
insight: Start from vertex form y = a(x - 2)^2 - 3 and plug in the point: 5 = a(4 - 2)^2 - 3, so 4a = 8 and a = 2. Assuming a = 1 is the trap.
visual: A parabola pinned at its vertex (2, -3) stretches taller like a spring until it passes through (4, 5), and the stretch readout settles at 2.
payoff: Quadratic from a vertex and a point
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Vertex plus one point gives the whole parabola.

title: The 1996 SAT question a 17-year-old proved wrong
hook: In 1996, a 17-year-old proved an SAT math answer key wrong.
insight: The question used a letter, a, and the key quietly assumed a was positive; Colin Rizzio showed that if a can be negative, the answer is 'cannot be determined'. Scores were raised for up to 45,000 students, and the lesson stands: a letter can be negative unless the question says otherwise.
visual: A number line with a slider for a glides from positive into negative, an illustrative comparison of a^2 and a^3 flips as a crosses zero, and a date card reads October 1996.
payoff: Questions that hinge on a constant's sign
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. One unstated assumption once raised about 45,000 SAT scores.

title: The percent swap: 4% of 75 is the same as 75% of 4
hook: What is 4% of 75? Flip it and it takes one second.
insight: a% of b is a times b divided by 100, and multiplication ignores order, so a% of b always equals b% of a. 4% of 75 equals 75% of 4, which is 3.
visual: A 4-by-75 rectangle labeled area 300 rotates a quarter turn so its side labels swap, the area stays 300, and a divide-by-100 chip turns it into 3.
payoff: fast percent-of arithmetic and answer checks
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. This percent swap makes the easy ones instant.

title: What is 30% of 20% of 500? Do it in your head
hook: What is 30% of 20% of 500? You have ten seconds.
insight: Of means times, so 30% of 20% is 0.3 x 0.2 = 0.06, which is 6%. 6% of 500 is 30.
visual: A 10-by-10 square shades a 20% strip in wash, 30% of that strip darkens to accent, and the 6 dark cells out of 100 snap into the label 6% before scaling up to 500.
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Try this percent-of-a-percent in ten seconds.

title: 18 is what percent of 24? Translate it word for word
hook: 18 is what percent of 24? Read it as an equation.
insight: Is means equals, of means times, and what percent means p/100. So 18 = (p/100) x 24, and p = 1,800 / 24 = 75.
visual: Each word of the sentence drops onto its symbol in place, is becomes =, of becomes x, what percent becomes p/100, and the equation solves to 75 in accent.
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Translate any percent sentence straight into an equation.

title: On SAT fill-in answers, never type the % sign
hook: The answer is 25%. What exactly do you type in the box?
insight: The student-produced response directions say not to enter symbols such as a percent sign, comma or dollar sign. If the question asks what percent, enter the number in front of the % sign, 25, not 0.25.
visual: An answer box shows 25% with the % struck in accent, then 0.25 struck, then 25 settles in as the directions line about symbols fades in above.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Don't lose a right answer to the % sign.

title: Which grew more, the town or the city? Depends on one word
hook: Town: 100 to 150. City: 10,000 to 10,500. Which grew more?
insight: The city added more people, 500 versus 50, but the town grew more in percent, 50% versus 5%. Percent change measures growth relative to the start, so check whether the question asks for an amount or a percent.
visual: Two bars of very different heights each grow a blue cap; the caps line up to compare 50 with 500, then each cap is laid against its own bar to show 50% against 5%.
payoff: greatest percent increase from a table
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Amount or percent? Table questions turn on that word.

title: Percent change in one step: divide new by old, subtract 1
hook: A price goes from $45 to $63. What is the percent increase?
insight: Divide new by old: 63 / 45 = 1.4. The 1 is the original whole and the leftover 0.4 is the change, so the price rose 40%.
visual: The fraction 63/45 collapses into the chip 1.4, the 1 peels off as the original whole, and the remaining 0.4 slides over to become 40%.
payoff: percent increase or decrease from two values
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. One division gives every percent change.

skill: Ratios, rates, proportional relationships, and units
title: 6 miles per hour in feet per second, with zero guessing
hook: A runner goes 6 miles per hour. How many feet per second?
insight: Multiply by fractions equal to 1, each placed so the unwanted unit cancels: 6 mi/h x 5,280 ft/mi x 1 h/3,600 s = 8.8 feet per second.
visual: Three fraction chips line up, miles cross out against miles and hours against hours like canceling variables, and only ft/s is left beside 8.8.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Every unit conversion is this one chain.

skill: Ratios, rates, proportional relationships, and units
title: Drive there at 60 mph, back at 40. Average speed isn't 50
hook: You drive 120 miles at 60 mph, then back at 40 mph. Average speed?
insight: Average speed is total distance over total time: 240 miles in 2 + 3 = 5 hours is 48 mph. You spend more time at the slow speed, so it counts more.
visual: A time bar fills 2 hours at 60 and 3 hours at 40, the longer slow segment visibly outweighs the fast one, and the balance marker settles at 48 beside a struck 50.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Averaging rates is the trap. Use total over total.

skill: Ratios, rates, proportional relationships, and units
title: Which is faster: a 4-minute mile or 15 mph?
hook: Which is faster: one mile in 4 minutes, or 15 miles per hour?
insight: They are the same. Flip minutes per mile into miles per hour: 60 minutes / 4 minutes per mile = 15 miles in an hour. A rate turns upside down when you swap what's on top.
visual: A clock ticks 4 minutes per mile, fifteen copies of that 4-minute block tile one 60-minute hour, and the 15 lights up next to 15 mph.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Flip a rate the right way every time.

title: Three doors, one car. Should you switch? The Monty Hall answer
hook: Pick one of three doors. The host opens a goat door. Switch?
insight: Yes: switching wins 2/3 of the time. Your first pick is right only 1/3 of the time, and whenever it's wrong, the host's reveal leaves the car behind the other closed door.
visual: Three doors split into your 1/3 and a blue 2/3 bracket over the other two; the host opens one goat door and the whole 2/3 slides onto the single remaining door.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Warm up for conditional probability with this famous puzzle.

skill: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error
title: A poll says 52% plus or minus 3%. Is she winning?
hook: A poll shows 52% support, margin of error 3%. Is she winning?
insight: You can't conclude it. The plausible range is 49% to 55%, and part of it is below 50%. A claim is supported only if it holds across the whole interval.
visual: A bracket from 49 to 55 lies over a number line with a dashed 50% line through it, and the slice below 50 turns blue as the words can't conclude appear.
payoff: which conclusion a margin of error supports
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Check the whole interval before you trust a claim.

skill: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error
title: The 2.4 million-person poll that picked the wrong president
hook: In 1936, a poll of 2.4 million people predicted Landon would beat Roosevelt.
insight: The Literary Digest drew names largely from phone books and car registrations and counted only the ballots people chose to mail back, so its sample leaned toward Landon. Roosevelt won 46 of 48 states: a huge biased sample is still biased.
visual: A giant cloud of 2.4 million dots fills the page but only from one corner of the population map, while a far smaller, evenly spread sample lands near the true result.
payoff: sampling bias and who results generalize to
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Sample size can't fix a biased sample. This poll proved it.

skill: Evaluating statistical claims: observational studies and experiments
title: Berkeley 1973: men were admitted more, until you split by department
hook: In 1973, Berkeley admitted 44% of men but only 35% of women.
insight: Within most departments, women were admitted at similar or higher rates; women had applied more often to departments that rejected most applicants. Combining groups of different sizes can reverse a comparison, which is Simpson's paradox.
visual: Two overall bars, 44% and 35%, split apart into department bar pairs; in most pairs the women's bar matches or tops the men's, while each department's width grows or shrinks to show where people applied.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Totals can mislead. Here's a real case where they did.

skill: Evaluating statistical claims: observational studies and experiments
title: Bombers came back with holes in the wings. Where do you add armor?
hook: Returning WWII bombers had bullet holes in the wings. Where should armor go?
insight: Where the returning planes have no holes. Abraham Wald's WWII insight: the data only includes planes that survived, so planes hit in other spots, like the engines, never came back to be counted.
visual: A plane outline fills with ink dots on the wings and tail, then ghost outlines of the planes that never returned fade in with their holes on the engines, which turn blue.
payoff: biased samples and who data represents
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Ask who's missing from the data. Here's the classic case.

title: A ball in a box fills less than you think
hook: A ball fits exactly in a cube. What fraction does it fill?
insight: Just over half: pi/6, about 52%. With edge 6 the ball has radius 3 and volume 36pi, about 113, against the cube's 216.
visual: A sphere inflates inside a wireframe cube until it touches all six faces, and the fill readout settles at 52%.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Guess the fraction before you watch.

title: A cone 3 times taller than a cylinder. Which holds more?
hook: Same radius, but the cone is 3 times taller. Which holds more?
insight: Neither: they hold exactly the same, because the cone's 1/3 cancels its triple height. 1/3 x pi r^2 x 3h = pi r^2 h.
visual: Water pours from the tall cone into the short cylinder and fills it exactly to the brim, with the two formulas cancelling on screen.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. One third of three times is one. Watch it pour.

title: A painted cube cut into 27. How many have no paint?
hook: A painted 3x3x3 cube is cut into 27 cubes. How many have no paint?
insight: Just 1, the hidden center cube. The rest are 8 corners with three painted faces, 12 edges with two and 6 face centers with one: 8 + 12 + 6 + 1 = 27.
visual: The cube explodes outward into 27 small cubes that sort themselves into groups of 8, 12 and 6, leaving one bare cube floating in the middle.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Count the hidden cube before you watch.

title: Two crescents versus a triangle: which has more area?
hook: Two crescents or the right triangle between them: which has more area?
insight: They are equal. By Pythagoras the semicircles on the legs add up to the semicircle on the hypotenuse, so removing the shared pieces leaves crescents equal to the triangle: legs 6 and 8 give 24 each way.
visual: Semicircles grow on a right triangle's three sides, the big one folds over the two small ones, and the overlapping slivers cancel until the two crescents and the triangle both read 24.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Crescents or triangle? Make your guess first.

title: The five tips of any star add to 180
hook: Draw any five-pointed star. What do its five tip angles add to?
insight: Always 180. Lay a pencil along one edge and rotate it through each tip in turn: after five tips it points backward, a half turn.
visual: A pencil rides along the star, pivoting at each tip through that tip's angle, and ends pointing the opposite way as the sum chip reads 180.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Guess the star's angle sum before the pencil turns.

title: The altitude to the hypotenuse in one step
hook: Right triangle with legs 6 and 8. Altitude to the hypotenuse?
insight: Write the area two ways: 1/2 x 6 x 8 = 1/2 x 10 x h, so h = 48 / 10 = 4.8. It is always leg times leg over hypotenuse.
visual: The triangle rotates until the hypotenuse is the base, the area chip 24 stays put, and the new height drops in at 4.8.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Area two ways finds any altitude.

title: Measure a tree with its shadow
hook: A 6-foot person casts a 4-foot shadow. A tree's shadow is 30 feet. Height?
insight: Sun rays are parallel, so the two triangles are similar: height is 1.5 times shadow, and the tree is 45 feet.
visual: Parallel sun rays sweep down at one angle, and the person's small triangle slides along the ground and scales up into the tree's triangle.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Parallel rays mean similar triangles.

title: SAT figures are drawn to scale. Use that
hook: Stuck on an angle question? The figure itself can rule out answers.
insight: Digital SAT figures are drawn to scale unless the question says otherwise, so a clearly acute angle cannot be 125 or 145. Estimate from the picture first, then compute.
visual: An arc overlays the figure's angle and reads about 50, and the two obtuse answer choices are struck in blue before any algebra starts.
urgent_hook: Test day for {test}. Glance at the figure first. It is drawn to scale.

title: Find r^2 without a square root
hook: Center (2, -3), passing through (5, 1). What is the circle's equation?
insight: Plug the point into the left side and it hands you r^2 directly: (5 - 2)^2 + (1 + 3)^2 = 9 + 16 = 25. The equation is (x - 2)^2 + (y + 3)^2 = 25.
visual: The point (5, 1) drops into the equation's blanks, the gaps 3 and 4 square into 9 and 16, and the right side fills with 25 as the circle draws through the point.
payoff: Writing a circle equation from a point
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Plug the point in. The right side writes itself.

title: What the SAT reference sheet leaves out
hook: The reference sheet gives you formulas. Here are four it leaves out.
insight: It leaves out the circle equation (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2, arcs and sectors as fractions of 360, sin x = cos(90 - x), and the scale rule k, k^2, k^3. Everything else, from cone volume to the 30-60-90 triangle, is on the sheet.
visual: The reference sheet appears as a printed card, then four blank lines beneath it fill in one at a time with the missing rules in blue.
payoff: Every geometry question on test day
urgent_hook: {test} is in {days} days. Memorize the four rules the reference sheet skips.

title: Your PSAT math score is already on the SAT scale
hook: You got a 600 on PSAT math. What does that mean for the SAT?
insight: The PSAT/NMSQT and the SAT share one score scale, so a 600 marks the same skill on both; College Board describes a PSAT score as the score you would have earned on the SAT that day. The PSAT section just tops out at 760 instead of 800.
visual: Two mono rulers align, 200 to 800 for the SAT and 160 to 760 for the PSAT on the same scale, and a dot at 600 drops straight down from one ruler to the other without moving sideways.
payoff: planning SAT math prep from a PSAT score
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Your fall PSAT math score is your starting line.

title: What the SAT reference sheet does NOT give you
hook: The reference sheet gives you 12 formulas. These six are missing.
insight: Not on the sheet: slope (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1), the circle equation (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2, the vertex x = -b/2a, the quadratic formula with its discriminant, SOH-CAH-TOA, and percent change = change/original. Everything else geometric is on the sheet, so memorize these six.
visual: The reference sheet draws on the left, then six blank cards slide in on the right and fill one by one with the missing formulas while the sheet's own formulas dim to gray.
payoff: questions that need a formula you must bring yourself
urgent_hook: {test} is in {days} days. Memorize the six formulas the sheet leaves out.

title: The words that mark a hard SAT math question
hook: 'Positive constant.' 'Exactly one.' 'Greatest possible value.' What do they signal?
insight: In the official bank, 23 of 28 questions saying 'positive constant' are rated hard, as are 14 of 15 saying 'exactly one' and 11 of 12 asking for a minimum or greatest possible value. Each phrase is a condition to use: a sign restriction, a discriminant or tangency, or an extreme at a vertex or boundary.
visual: A question's text sits on the page and three phrases lift out in accent, each dropping onto its matching picture: a number line cut at zero, a line grazing a parabola, and a vertex dot at the top of an arch.
urgent_hook: Retaking on {date}? Learn to spot these three phrases first.

title: The units digit of 7^623, in five seconds
hook: What is the last digit of 7 to the 623rd power?
insight: 3. Last digits of powers of 7 cycle 7, 9, 3, 1 every four steps; 623 = 4 x 155 + 3, so 7^623 ends like 7^3 = 343.
visual: A clock face with four positions 7, 9, 3, 1 spins one notch per power while a mono counter races to 623, landing on 3 after 155 full laps plus three notches.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Warm up with a five-second pattern puzzle.

title: 8% of 25 is the same as 25% of 8. Here's why.
hook: What is 8% of 25? Three seconds. Flip it.
insight: 2. a% of b = a x b / 100 = b% of a, so 8% of 25 = 25% of 8, which is a quarter of 8. It is one 8-by-25 rectangle read from either side.
visual: An 8 by 25 rectangle of area 200 is labeled from the left as '8% of 25' and from the bottom as '25% of 8', then divides into 100 equal tiles, each worth 2.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Flip any percent and do it in your head.

title: sqrt(6 + sqrt(6 + sqrt(6 + ...))) forever equals exactly 3
hook: The square root of 6 plus the square root of 6, forever. Value?
insight: 3. Call it x; the part under the first root is the whole thing again, so x = sqrt(6 + x), x^2 = x + 6, (x - 3)(x + 2) = 0, and since x is positive, x = 3.
visual: The nested expression zooms into itself, a box around the inner copy relabels as x, and a cobweb staircase between y = sqrt(6 + x) and y = x spirals into the point (3, 3).
payoff: rejecting the extraneous root in a radical equation
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. This infinite root takes one line to solve.

title: The 1982 SAT question with no right answer
hook: Circle A, one-third the radius of B, rolls around B. How many turns?
insight: On the May 1, 1982 SAT the keyed answer was 3, from the choices 3/2, 3, 6, 9/2 and 9, but the true answer is 4: three turns from the distance rolled plus one more from traveling around B. Three students caught it, and about 300,000 math scores were recalculated.
visual: A small coin with a painted radius rolls around a coin three times its size while a mono counter ticks 1, 2, 3; the path unrolls flat to show 3, then the trip around the circle adds the fourth turn in accent.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Even the SAT got this circle question wrong once.

title: A 17-year-old proved the 1980 PSAT wrong with two pyramids
hook: Glue a triangular pyramid to a square pyramid. How many faces?
insight: In October 1980 the PSAT keyed 7, nine faces minus the two glued ones, but with all edges equal two pairs of faces line up flat and merge, leaving 5. Daniel Lowen, 17, of Cocoa Beach, Florida, showed it, and about a quarter million scores were raised.
visual: An orthographic wireframe tetrahedron slides onto a square pyramid's side face, the glued faces vanish, then two pairs of neighboring triangles flatten into shared planes in accentWash and the face counter drops from 7 to 5.
payoff: 3D visualization and counting faces for surface area
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Count these faces; the test makers once got it wrong.

title: Add 1 to 100 in ten seconds: the staircase trick
hook: 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + 100. Ten seconds. Go.
insight: 5050. Copy the staircase, flip the copy, and fit the two together: they make a 100 by 101 rectangle, so one staircase is 100 x 101 / 2 = 5050.
visual: A staircase of 100 columns draws in ink, a rotated copy in accentWash slides on top, and together they lock into a 100 by 101 rectangle that splits in half.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. A ten-second warmup that teaches averages.

title: Is 0.999... repeating exactly equal to 1?
hook: Zero point nine nine nine, forever. Is it less than 1?
insight: It equals 1 exactly. 1/3 = 0.333..., and three of those are both 0.999... and 3/3 = 1. If the two numbers differed, some number would fit between them, and none does.
visual: A unit bar fills by 9/10, then 9/100 of the gap, then 9/1000, the gap shrinking to nothing, then three 0.333... bars stack into one whole bar.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Settle the 0.999... argument in one picture.

title: A rope around the Earth, raised 1 meter. How much longer?
hook: A rope hugs the Earth. Raise it 1 meter everywhere. Extra rope?
insight: Only 2 pi, about 6.28 meters, whatever the planet's size: C = 2 pi r is a line in r, so adding 1 to r adds 2 pi to C.
visual: A rope circle around a huge ink Earth grows outward by a hairline gap of 1, a readout shows +6.28 m, then the Earth shrinks to a coin and the readout stays at +6.28 m.
payoff: circumference as a linear function of radius
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Guess first, then watch the circle prove you wrong.

title: Fold paper 42 times and it reaches the Moon
hook: A sheet 0.1 mm thick, folded 42 times. How tall?
insight: About 440,000 km, past the Moon's average distance of about 384,000 km: each fold doubles the stack, so it is 0.1 mm x 2^42. Doubling, not adding, is what exponential means.
visual: A thin bar doubles in height with each fold beside a mono counter, staying tiny for 20 folds, then the view pulls back as the stack shoots past a mountain, a plane and finally the Moon at fold 42.
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. See why exponential growth always wins.

title: 111,111,111 squared is a palindrome. Why?
hook: What is 111,111,111 squared? Look at the shape.
insight: 12,345,678,987,654,321. Multiplying ones by ones fills a 9 by 9 grid of 1s, and its diagonals hold 1, 2, ..., 9, ..., 2, 1 ones, small enough that nothing carries.
visual: A 9 by 9 grid of ones draws, then diagonal stripes sweep across it counting 1, 2, 3 up to 9 at the middle and back down, each count dropping into its digit place.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. A palindrome hiding inside a multiplication grid.

title: 142857 times 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 just rotates its digits
hook: Multiply 142857 by 2. Then by 3. Notice anything?
insight: 285714, 428571, 571428, 714285, 857142: the same six digits rotated, because 142857 is the repeating block of 1/7, and 2/7 through 6/7 start that same cycle at different points. Times 7 gives 999999.
visual: The digits 1 4 2 8 5 7 sit on a ring; each multiplication spins the ring to a new starting point, then x7 fills every slot with 9.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. The strangest six-digit number in arithmetic.

title: What's the angle between clock hands at 3:15? Not zero.
hook: At 3:15, what is the angle between the clock's hands?
insight: 7.5 degrees. The hour hand doesn't wait at 3: it moves 0.5 degrees per minute, so at 3:15 it sits at 97.5 degrees while the minute hand is at 90.
visual: A clock face draws, the minute hand sweeps to the 3, and the hour hand creeps a quarter of the way toward 4, opening a thin accentWash wedge labeled 7.5 degrees.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. A two-hand puzzle about rates hiding in a clock.

title: The Monty Hall problem: should you switch doors?
hook: Three doors, one car. You pick, a goat is shown. Switch?
insight: Switch: you win 2/3 of the time. Your first pick is right only 1/3 of the time, and the host's reveal never changes that, so the other 2/3 collapses onto the one remaining door.
visual: Three doors split into a 1/3 region and a 2/3 region, the host opens a goat door inside the 2/3 region, and its whole share slides onto the remaining door in accent; then the same picture replays with 100 doors.
payoff: probability as a fraction of outcomes
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. The most argued probability puzzle, in one picture.

title: 23 people in a room: two probably share a birthday
hook: How many people until two probably share a birthday?
insight: 23. With 23 people there are 23 x 22 / 2 = 253 pairs, and the chance that every birthday differs falls to about 49%, so a shared birthday is about 51%.
visual: Dots for people appear one by one and every pair joins with a thin gray line, the line count racing to 253, while a probability bar for 'all different' slides below the 50% mark at the 23rd dot.
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. A probability surprise you can test at school tomorrow.

title: You will see "What does 30 represent?" on the SAT
hook: Almost every SAT asks what a number in a linear model means.
insight: Plug in 0 to read the constant: it is the value before anything happens. Then add 1 to the input to read the coefficient: it is the change for each one more unit.
visual: Three models slide past (gym, phone plan, savings), each constant lights up where its graph meets the y-axis and each coefficient lights up as one step of a staircase.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. This question type is almost guaranteed.

title: f(3) = 7 is just the point (3, 7)
hook: f(3) = 7. This notation scares people. It's just a dot.
insight: f(3) = 7 means that when x is 3, the height of the graph is 7, so the point (3, 7) is on the graph. Every f statement is a coordinate in disguise.
visual: The symbols f(3) = 7 slide apart, the 3 drops onto the x-axis, the 7 onto the y-axis, and dashed guides meet at a blue dot on the line.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Every f(a) = b is a point. Use it.

title: You will see "the point (a, b) lies on the line" on the SAT
hook: The point (2, 7) is on y = kx + 1. What is k?
insight: A point on a line makes its equation true, so substitute both coordinates: 7 = 2k + 1, so k = 3. The question bank has about 48 of these.
visual: The dot (2, 7) drops onto the grid, its coordinates fly into the x and y slots of the equation, and k resolves to 3 as the line swings through the dot.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Plug in both coordinates. This one is nearly certain.

skill: Systems of two linear equations in two variables
title: The scary no-solution formula just means "same slope, new line"
hook: a/d = b/e, but not c/f. This rule just means parallel.
insight: a/d = b/e rearranges to -a/b = -d/e, which says the two slopes are equal. The c/f part only asks whether the lines also share a point: equal means one line drawn twice, unequal means parallel lines that never meet.
visual: The two equations sit stacked, the first two ratio pairs light up as matching slope triangles, then the third ratio decides whether the lines merge or stay apart.
payoff: every no-solution and infinitely-many system question
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Decode this one rule and two question types fall.

title: Factor x^4 - 81 completely. Most people stop too early
hook: Factor x to the fourth minus 81 completely.
insight: It is a difference of squares twice: x^4 - 81 = (x^2 + 9)(x^2 - 9) = (x^2 + 9)(x + 3)(x - 3). Writing (x^2 - 9)^2, or stopping at x^2 - 9, is the trap.
visual: x^4 - 81 splits into a sum and a difference of x^2 and 9, then the difference splits again into (x + 3)(x - 3) while the sum stays put in gray.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Factor completely means keep going.

skill: Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables
title: x^2/(x - 3) = 9/(x - 3). The answer is not 3
hook: Solve x squared over x minus 3 equals 9 over x minus 3.
insight: Clearing the denominators gives x^2 = 9, so x = 3 or -3. But x = 3 makes the denominator 0, so it is excluded, and the only solution is -3.
visual: Both denominators fade away, x^2 = 9 splits into 3 and -3, then x = 3 is struck in blue as it zeroes the denominator, leaving -3.
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Always check what makes the denominator zero.

skill: Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables
title: (x + 2)^2 = (2x - 1)^2 has two solutions, not one
hook: Solve x plus 2, squared, equals 2x minus 1, squared.
insight: Equal squares mean the insides are equal or opposite: x + 2 = 2x - 1 gives x = 3, and x + 2 = -(2x - 1) gives x = -1/3. Dropping the second case loses an answer.
visual: The two parabolas y = (x + 2)^2 and y = (2x - 1)^2 cross at x = -1/3 and x = 3, and the forgotten second case lights up in blue.
urgent_hook: Planning a retake on {date}? Missing second cases like this costs hard-module points.

title: f(t) = 100(1.04)^(3t): 4% growth every how many months?
hook: f(t) = 100(1.04)^(3t), t in years. It grows 4% every how many months?
insight: 3t means the 4% growth happens 3 times per year, so once every 12/3 = 4 months. Answering 3 mixes up the count per year with the gap between them.
visual: A year bar splits into three 4-month segments, a 1.04 stamp lands at each boundary, and 3 is struck while 4 lights up in blue.
urgent_hook: Retaking on {date}? Learn to read the period hidden in the exponent.

title: f(x) = (x - 1)(x + 4) and f(c - 2) = 0. Find c
hook: f(x) = (x-1)(x+4) and f(c-2) = 0. Find c.
insight: f is zero only when its input is 1 or -4, so set the input c - 2 equal to each: c = 3 or c = -2. Answering 1 or -4 solves for the wrong letter.
visual: The two zeros of f light up on the axis, the input box c - 2 slides onto each one, and c resolves to 3 and -2 as the graph shifts 2 to the right.
urgent_hook: Retaking on {date}? Set the inside equal to each zero. That's the move.

skill: Ratios, rates, proportional relationships, and units
title: If 6x = 4y, what is x/y? Not 6/4
hook: If 6x = 4y, what is x/y?
insight: Divide both sides by 6y: x/y = 4/6 = 2/3. The bigger coefficient sits on the smaller variable, so the ratio flips and x is the smaller one.
visual: Six x-blocks balance four y-blocks on a beam, the y-blocks are visibly longer, and the fraction 6/4 flips to 4/6 and reduces to 2/3.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. This ratio flip catches strong students.

skill: One-variable data: distributions and measures of center and spread
title: Everyone gets 5 bonus points. What happens to the SD?
hook: Every score gets 5 bonus points. What happens to the standard deviation?
insight: Nothing. The mean rises by 5, but every score moves with it, so every distance from the mean stays the same. Multiplying every score by 2 would double the SD.
visual: A dot plot with distance sticks to its mean slides 5 units right as one rigid piece, the sticks keep their lengths, and the SD readout never changes.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Shift the data, keep the spread. Learn why.

title: P(junior or athlete) is not 50% + 40%
hook: 50 juniors, 40 athletes, 30 junior athletes, 100 students. P(junior or athlete)?
insight: Adding 50 and 40 counts the 30 junior athletes twice. Subtract the overlap once: (50 + 40 - 30)/100 = 0.6.
visual: Two overlapping circles of 50 and 40 dots slide together, the shared 30 dots glow double, one copy fades out, and 60 of 100 remain blue.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. 'Or' means don't count the overlap twice.

title: Draw 2 from 3 red, 2 blue. P(both red) isn't (3/5)^2
hook: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue. Draw two. Chance both are red?
insight: After the first red is gone, only 2 reds remain among 4 marbles: 3/5 x 2/4 = 3/10, not 9/25. Without replacement, the second fraction changes.
visual: Five marbles sit in a row, one red leaves the bag, the fraction 3/5 is joined by 2/4 as the bag visibly shrinks, and 9/25 is struck.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Once a marble leaves the bag, the odds change.

skill: Evaluating statistical claims: observational studies and experiments
title: Volunteers were randomly assigned. Does the result apply to everyone?
hook: 200 volunteers, randomly assigned to sleep 8 or 6 hours. What can you conclude?
insight: Random assignment supports cause, so more sleep caused the difference for subjects like these volunteers. But they weren't randomly sampled from a population, so you can't generalize to all people.
visual: A crowd of volunteers splits by coin flips into two groups and a cause checkmark appears over them, then the frame zooms out to a large population outside the crowd that stays gray beside a struck everyone.
urgent_hook: Retaking {test}? This is one of the hardest data questions. Here's the rule.

title: Skip the distance formula on this triangle
hook: Corners (1, 1), (9, 1) and (4, 7). What is the triangle's area?
insight: Two corners share y = 1, so that side is a flat base of 8, and the height is straight up to y = 7, which is 6. Area = 1/2 x 8 x 6 = 24, with no slanted lengths needed.
visual: A distance-formula calculation starts and is struck, then the flat side lights up along a grid line and a dashed vertical drops from (4, 7) onto it as the area chip resolves to 24.
payoff: Triangle area on the coordinate plane
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Look for a flat side before computing anything.

title: Three consecutive integers add to 72. The middle one is 24
hook: Three consecutive integers add to 72. Find them in two seconds.
insight: Consecutive numbers balance around the middle one, so the middle is the average: 72/3 = 24, giving 23, 24 and 25. No equation needed.
visual: Three bars of heights 23, 24 and 25 stand side by side, the tallest hands one unit to the shortest, and all three level at 24.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. The middle number is the average.

skill: Systems of two linear equations in two variables
title: Which point solves this system for every value of r?
hook: 2x-y=4 and 6x-3y=12. Which point works for every r?
insight: The second equation is 3 times the first, so they are the same line, y = 2x - 4. Every point (r, 2r - 4) solves both, not just one point.
visual: Both lines draw and land on top of each other, then a dot labeled (r, 2r - 4) glides along the doubled line as r ticks through 0, 1 and 2.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. When the lines match, every point answers.

skill: Linear inequalities in one or two variables
title: The origin test: know which side to shade in one second
hook: y > 2x - 1. Shade above or below? Test (0, 0).
insight: Plug in (0, 0): 0 > -1 is true, so shade the side that contains the origin. If it comes out false, shade the other side; if the line passes through the origin, test another point.
visual: The line draws, a dot drops at the origin, the check 0 > -1 inks true, and the wash floods the origin's side of the plane.
urgent_hook: {test} is today. One plug-in picks the shaded side.

skill: Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables
title: x + y = 10 and xy = 20. What is 1/x + 1/y?
hook: x + y = 10 and xy = 20. What is 1/x + 1/y?
insight: Add the fractions: 1/x + 1/y = (x + y)/(xy) = 10/20 = 1/2. Solving for x and y gives the messy roots 5 + sqrt(5) and 5 - sqrt(5), which the question never needed.
visual: The two unit fractions slide over a shared denominator xy, the numerator gathers into x + y, and 10 over 20 collapses to 1/2 in blue.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Combine first. Solving is the trap.

skill: Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables
title: C times C times C times C equals C + C + C + C. Find C^6
hook: C*C*C*C = C+C+C+C, and C is positive. What is C^6?
insight: The left side is C^4 and the right side is 4C, so dividing by the positive C gives C^3 = 4. Then C^6 = (C^3)^2 = 16, with no cube roots needed.
visual: Four C's multiplied collapse into C^4 while four C's added collapse into 4C, one C cancels from each side in blue, and C^3 = 4 squares into 16.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Can you tell multiplying from adding when it counts?

title: 9^0 + 0^9 + 9^1 = ? Most people say 9
hook: Quick: what is 9^0 + 0^9 + 9^1?
insight: Walk down the powers of 9 (81, then 9, then divide by 9 once more) and 9^0 = 1, while 0^9 is nine zeros multiplied, so 0. The total is 1 + 0 + 9 = 10.
visual: A staircase of 9^2, 9^1 and 9^0 descends with a divide-by-9 arrow at each step and lands on 1, while 0^9 collapses to 0 beside it.
payoff: Zero exponents and powers of zero
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Settle the zero exponent for good before you sit down.

title: Which is bigger: (2^3)^2 or 2^(3^2)?
hook: Which is bigger: (2^3)^2 or 2^(3^2)?
insight: (2^3)^2 multiplies the exponents, 2^6 = 64, but 2^(3^2) puts 3^2 = 9 in the exponent first, 2^9 = 512. A power of a power multiplies; a tower is read from the top down.
visual: The parentheses glow in turn: the first version regroups into two blocks of three 2s making 64, the second unrolls into nine 2s making 512.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Parentheses change everything in this one.

title: 101^2 - 99^2 in five seconds, no calculator
hook: Can you do 101 squared minus 99 squared in five seconds?
insight: a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b), so 101^2 - 99^2 = 200 times 2 = 400. No squaring needed.
visual: A 101-sided square with a 99-sided square cut from its corner leaves a thin L, which slides into a 200-by-2 rectangle that reads 400.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Difference of squares, done entirely in your head.

skill: Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables
title: (1/4)^x = 32. Why x has to be negative
hook: If one-fourth to the x equals 32, what is x?
insight: 1/4 is 2^-2 and 32 is 2^5, so 2^(-2x) = 2^5 and x = -5/2. A fraction base needs a negative exponent to grow past 1.
visual: 1/4 rewrites as 2^-2 with a flip arrow, 32 as 2^5, the exponents line up as -2x = 5, and x = -5/2 lands in accent.
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Fractions are just negative powers. Use that on test day.

title: Turn every root into an exponent: x^2 times cube root of x
hook: Which is equivalent to x squared times the cube root of x?
insight: Write the root as a power, x^(1/3), then add exponents: x^2 times x^(1/3) = x^(2 + 1/3) = x^(7/3). Multiplying the exponents into x^(2/3) is the trap.
visual: The cube-root sign dissolves into a small 1/3 exponent, slides next to the 2, and the exponents add into 7/3 while x^(2/3) is struck.
payoff: Finding the exponent that makes expressions equivalent
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Turn roots into exponents, then just add.

title: Which is bigger: sqrt(2) + sqrt(3) or sqrt(10)?
hook: Which is bigger: root 2 plus root 3, or root 10?
insight: Square both: (sqrt(2) + sqrt(3))^2 = 5 + 2sqrt(6), about 9.90, while (sqrt(10))^2 = 10. So sqrt(10) wins, barely: about 3.162 against 3.146.
visual: Two bars look almost equal, both get squared into areas, the 5 + 2sqrt(6) square falls just short of the 10 square, and the gap glows in blue.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. When roots refuse to compare, square them.

title: The 15 powers worth memorizing before the SAT
hook: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64. These hide in many SAT exponent questions.
insight: Know the powers of 2 up to 64, of 3 up to 243 and of 5 up to 625. Spotting 32 as 2^5 or 81 as 3^4 is the first move in nearly every same-base rewrite.
visual: Three ladders of 2s, 3s and 5s climb up the page, and numbers pulled from sample questions, 32, 81 and 125, fly onto their rungs in blue.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Memorize these 15 powers tonight.

title: What is 4^5 times 25^5? Pair the bases
hook: What is 4 to the fifth times 25 to the fifth?
insight: Same exponent, so pair the bases: 4^5 times 25^5 = (4 times 25)^5 = 100^5 = 10^10, ten billion. 100^10 and 29^5 are the traps.
visual: Five 4s and five 25s zip together into five pairs, each pair snaps into 100, and the row of five 100s reads as a 1 followed by ten zeros.
payoff: Products of powers with equal exponents
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Matching exponents? Pair the bases first.

title: (sqrt(5) + sqrt(3))(sqrt(5) - sqrt(3)) is a whole number
hook: Multiply root 5 plus root 3 by root 5 minus root 3.
insight: It is a difference of squares: (a + b)(a - b) = a^2 - b^2 = 5 - 3 = 2. The cross terms cancel, so the roots disappear completely.
visual: An area grid of sqrt(5) + sqrt(3) by sqrt(5) - sqrt(3) fills its four cells, the two cross cells cancel in blue, and a clean 2 remains.
payoff: Conjugates and difference of squares with radicals
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Conjugates make radicals vanish. Here's why.

title: x^2 - y^2 = 24 and x + y = 6. Find x - y fast
hook: x^2 - y^2 = 24, x + y = 6. Find x - y.
insight: Factor: x^2 - y^2 = (x + y)(x - y), so 24 = 6(x - y) and x - y = 4. You never need x = 5 and y = 1.
visual: x^2 - y^2 opens into (x + y)(x - y), the known 6 drops into the first factor, and 24 divided by 6 lights up 4.
payoff: Using factored structure instead of solving
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Factor first, and the system answers itself.

title: If x + 1/x = 3, what is x^2 + 1/x^2? Not 9
hook: x + 1/x = 3. What is x^2 + 1/x^2?
insight: Square the whole equation: (x + 1/x)^2 = x^2 + 2 + 1/x^2 = 9, because each cross term x times 1/x equals 1. So x^2 + 1/x^2 = 7.
visual: A square of side x + 1/x splits into four regions, the two cross pieces each read 1 and lift out in blue, leaving 9 - 2 = 7.
payoff: Squaring a sum to reach a target expression
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Square the whole thing. The cross term is the trick.

title: x + y = 10 and xy = 20. Find 1/x + 1/y without x
hook: x + y = 10 and xy = 20. What is 1/x + 1/y?
insight: Put the fractions over a common denominator: 1/x + 1/y = (x + y)/(xy) = 10/20 = 1/2. Solving for x and y would mean the irrational 5 plus or minus sqrt(5).
visual: 1/x and 1/y slide onto the shared denominator xy, the numerator becomes x + y, and the given 10 and 20 drop into place to read 1/2.
payoff: Rational expressions from sums and products
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Don't solve for x. Combine the fractions.

title: Which is bigger: sqrt(2) or the cube root of 3?
hook: Which is bigger: the square root of 2 or the cube root of 3?
insight: Raise both to the 6th power to clear the roots: (2^(1/2))^6 = 8 and (3^(1/3))^6 = 9. So the cube root of 3, about 1.442, beats sqrt(2), about 1.414.
visual: Both numbers enter a power machine set to 6, the roots dissolve, 8 and 9 come out as stacks of tiles, and the taller stack lights up in blue.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Two roots, different sizes. One move compares them.

title: 10^20 vs 20^10: the bigger exponent or the bigger base?
hook: Which is bigger: 10 to the 20th or 20 to the 10th?
insight: Split 20 into 2 times 10: 20^10 = 2^10 times 10^10, about 1,024 times 10^10, roughly 10^13. So 10^20 is bigger, by a factor of almost ten million.
visual: 20^10 splits into a row of ten 2s and a row of ten 10s, the 2s condense to about 1,000, and two strings of zeros line up with 10^20 running far past.
payoff: Comparing powers with different bases and exponents
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Bigger base or bigger exponent? Split it and see.

title: Is 2^30 more or less than a billion?
hook: Is 2 to the 30th more or less than a billion?
insight: 2^10 = 1,024, just over 1,000, so 2^30 = (2^10)^3 is just over 1,000^3, a billion. Exactly, it is 1,073,741,824.
visual: Thirty 2s group into three blocks of ten, each block collapses to 1,024, the three blocks line up beside three 1,000s, and the total ticks up to 1,073,741,824.
payoff: Estimating powers with a power of a power
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Estimate giant powers with one number: 1,024.

title: 5^(-2) or 2^(-5)? Negative exponents flip the winner
hook: Which is bigger: 5 to the negative 2 or 2 to the negative 5?
insight: Negative exponents flip, so compare 1/25 with 1/32. 2^5 = 32 is the bigger power, so its reciprocal is smaller, and 5^(-2) wins.
visual: 5^2 and 2^5 build as 25 and 32 tile squares, then both flip into slices of a unit square, and the 1/25 slice comes out wider in blue.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Negative exponents reverse the comparison. Here's why.

title: Rewrite (x + 5)/(x + 3) by splitting the top
hook: Which is equivalent to x plus 5 over x plus 3?
insight: Split the numerator to copy the denominator: x + 5 = (x + 3) + 2, so (x + 5)/(x + 3) = 1 + 2/(x + 3). Answer choices shaped like 1 + something come from this move.
visual: The numerator x + 5 breaks into an x + 3 block and a leftover 2, the matching block cancels with the bottom into a 1, and the 2 stays over x + 3.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Make the top look like the bottom.

title: How many integers b let x^2 + bx + 12 factor?
hook: x squared plus bx plus 12 factors with integers. How many b values work?
insight: b is the sum of two integers that multiply to 12: (1, 12), (2, 6) and (3, 4) give 13, 8 and 7, and their negatives give -13, -8 and -7. Six values in all.
visual: Twelve tiles rearrange into 1-by-12, 2-by-6 and 3-by-4 rectangles, each one's side lengths add into a b value, then the set mirrors into negatives.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Factor pairs answer this in seconds.

title: How many x-intercepts does x^2 - 4x + 7 have? Check the vertex
hook: How many x-intercepts does y = x^2 - 4x + 7 have?
insight: The vertex is at x = 2, where y = 4 - 8 + 7 = 3. The parabola opens up from a lowest point above the axis, so it never crosses: zero x-intercepts.
visual: The parabola's lowest point lights up at (2, 3), a dashed guide shows the gap of 3 above the axis, and the arms rise away without touching.
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. One point tells you how many intercepts.

skill: Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables
title: x + y = 7 and xy = 12. Solve it in your head
hook: x + y = 7 and xy = 12. What are x and y?
insight: Two numbers with sum 7 and product 12 are the roots of t^2 - 7t + 12 = 0, which factors as (t - 3)(t - 4). So x and y are 3 and 4, in either order.
visual: A sum bar of length 7 and a product rectangle of area 12 search through number pairs, then lock at 3 and 4 as t^2 - 7t + 12 writes itself.
payoff: Nonlinear systems with a sum and a product
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. A sum and a product make a quadratic.

skill: Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables
title: How many solutions does x^4 - 5x^2 + 4 = 0 have?
hook: How many solutions does x^4 - 5x^2 + 4 = 0 have?
insight: Treat x^2 as one chunk u: u^2 - 5u + 4 = 0, so u = 1 or 4. Then x^2 = 1 or 4 gives x = 1, -1, 2 and -2: four solutions.
visual: Every x^2 gets boxed and renamed u, a simple quadratic factors, then each box unpacks into a plus-minus pair as a W-shaped graph crosses the axis four times.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. A fourth power can be a quadratic in disguise.

skill: Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables
title: Two consecutive integers multiply to 132. Find them fast
hook: Two consecutive positive integers have a product of 132. What are they?
insight: Their product is close to a square, so take sqrt(132), about 11.5, and the integers straddle it: 11 and 12. Indeed 11 times 12 = 132, with no quadratic formula needed.
visual: A 132-tile rectangle reshapes toward a square of side about 11.5, then settles as an 11-by-12 rectangle with both side lengths lit in blue.
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Estimate with a square root, then check.

title: Rewrite 1000(1.2)^t to show the monthly growth rate
hook: 1000(1.2)^t grows 20% a year. What's the equivalent monthly rate?
insight: Put 12t in the exponent and take the 12th root of the base: 1000(1.2^(1/12))^(12t), about 1000(1.0153)^(12t). That is about 1.53% per month, not 20/12 = 1.67%.
visual: The base 1.2 splits into twelve equal multiplicative steps along a year bar, each step reads 1.0153, and their product reassembles to 1.2 at the year mark.
payoff: Equivalent exponential forms with different periods
urgent_hook: Retaking on {date}? This equivalent-form question separates top scores.

title: f(0) = 5 and f(2) = 45. Find f(3) for an exponential
hook: Exponential f has f(0) = 5 and f(2) = 45. What is f(3)?
insight: f(0) is the starting value, so a = 5, and two steps multiply by b^2 = 45/5 = 9, so b = 3. Then f(3) = 45 times 3 = 135.
visual: Points at x = 0 and x = 2 sit on the grid, two equal ratio arrows labeled times 3 connect them, and a third arrow climbs to 135 at x = 3.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Two points pin down any exponential. Here's how.

title: x^2 + bx + 11 has its minimum at x = 3. Find the minimum
hook: Minimum of x^2 + bx + 11 is at x = 3. Its value?
insight: The vertex is at -b/2 = 3, so b = -6. Then the minimum value is f(3) = 9 - 18 + 11 = 2.
visual: The axis line x = 3 drops into place, b resolves to -6 in the readout, and the parabola settles with its vertex at height 2 in blue.
urgent_hook: Retaking on {date}? Unknown constant plus a vertex takes two moves.

title: A parabola passes through (-2, 5) and (6, 5). Find the vertex x
hook: A parabola passes through negative 2, 5 and 6, 5. Where's its vertex?
insight: Equal heights sit mirror-symmetric about the axis, so the vertex's x is their average: (-2 + 6)/2 = 2. The shared 5 is a distraction.
visual: Two dots at height 5 sit on the grid, the parabola folds along a vertical line until they meet, and the fold line lands at x = 2.
payoff: Axis of symmetry from equal outputs
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Equal heights give you the axis for free.

title: Raise the price, lose customers. Where's the max revenue?
hook: $20 tickets sell 300. Each $1 raise loses 10 sales. Best price?
insight: Revenue is (20 + x)(300 - 10x), which is zero at x = -20 and x = 30, so the peak is halfway, at x = 5. That means a $25 price, 250 sales and $6,250 in revenue.
visual: A rectangle with width price and height sales reshapes as a price slider moves, its area traces a parabola, and the peak lands at $25 midway between the zeros.
urgent_hook: Retaking on {date}? This revenue model is a classic hard-module question.

title: Vertex at x = 4, zero at x = 1. Find c in x^2 + bx + c
hook: Vertex at x = 4, one zero at x = 1. What is c?
insight: Reflect the zero across the axis: 1 is 3 to the left of x = 4, so the other zero is 7. Then x^2 + bx + c = (x - 1)(x - 7), so c = 7 and b = -8.
visual: The dot at x = 1 reflects across the dashed axis x = 4 to land at x = 7, then the two zeros drop into factored form and multiply out to c = 7.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Reflect across the axis to find the missing zero.

title: x is 40% of y, y is 150% of z. x is what percent of z?
hook: x is 40% of y, y is 150% of z. Find x over z.
insight: Write each percent as a multiplier and chain them like unit conversions: x/z = (x/y)(y/z) = 0.4 x 1.5 = 0.6. So x is 60% of z.
visual: Two fraction chips, x/y = 0.4 and y/z = 1.5, slide together, the y's cross out like units, and the product chip 0.6 turns blue as 60%.
urgent_hook: {test} is in {days} days. Chain these percents like unit conversions.

title: Every percent change is one multiplication: 1.31 and 0.85
hook: Which expression shows b increased by 31%? Not 0.31b.
insight: Increasing by r keeps the whole b and adds rb, so the new value is (1 + r)b: a 31% increase is 1.31b. A 15% decrease keeps 85% of b, so it is 0.85b, not 0.15b.
visual: A bar labeled b grows a thin blue 0.31b sliver, the label b + 0.31b merges into 1.31b, then a second bar loses a 0.15b slice and its label collapses to 0.85b.
payoff: percent as a multiplier with variables
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Turn every percent into one multiplier tonight.

title: Discount first or tax first? Which way is cheaper?
hook: A $50 item: 20% off and 8% tax. Does the order matter?
insight: No. Each step multiplies, and multiplication works in any order: 50 x 0.8 x 1.08 = 50 x 1.08 x 0.8 = $43.20 either way.
visual: Two chains of multiplier chips, 0.8 then 1.08 and 1.08 then 0.8, swap places like train cars while the total chip stays at $43.20.
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Settle this cashier argument with one multiplication.

title: Buy 2 get 1 free, or 40% off? One is clearly better
hook: Buy two, get one free, or 40% off everything. Which saves more?
insight: Buy 2 get 1 free means you pay for 2 of every 3 items, so 1/3 is free: about 33.3% off. 40% off is the better deal.
visual: Three identical boxes appear, one turns blue as free and reads 1/3 = 33.3%, then a 40% bar slides up beside it and clearly overtops it.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Convert every deal to one percent and compare.

title: If 120% of x is 48, what is 80% of x? Skip finding x
hook: If 120% of x is 48, what is 80% of x?
insight: 80% is two thirds of 120%, so 80% of x is two thirds of 48, which is 32. You never need x itself, though x = 40 confirms it.
visual: A bar of twelve 10% cells labeled 48 shows each cell as 4, then the bar shrinks to eight cells and the readout counts down to 32.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Answer the percent they ask for, not the x.

title: Test-day percent check: bigger or smaller, before you calculate
hook: After a 15% raise, a price is $92. Was the original more or less?
insight: Less, so the answer must be under $92: 92 / 1.15 = $80. Deciding the direction first catches the classic slip of multiplying, 92 x 1.15 = $105.80, when you should divide.
visual: A number line with $92 marked shows an arrow that must point left; the struck $105.80 lands on the wrong side while $80 lands on the correct side in blue.
urgent_hook: {test} is today. Before any percent answer, decide: bigger or smaller?

skill: Ratios, rates, proportional relationships, and units
title: 3 boys for every 5 girls, and 12 more girls. How many kids?
hook: Boys to girls is 3 to 5, with 12 more girls than boys. Total?
insight: The gap between 5 parts and 3 parts is 2 parts, and that gap is 12 students, so one part is 6. The class has 8 parts, so 48 students: 18 boys and 30 girls.
visual: Three ink tiles and five blue tiles line up, the two extra blue tiles get bracketed as 12, each tile fills with 6 dots, and the total 48 appears.
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Use the gap between parts to crack ratio problems.

skill: One-variable data: distributions and measures of center and spread
title: You average 85 on 4 tests. What do you need to average 88?
hook: You average 85 on four tests. What score on the fifth makes 88?
insight: Work with totals: you need 5 x 88 = 440 points and have 4 x 85 = 340, so you need 100. Equivalently, the fifth test must cover 88 plus the 3-point shortfall of each of the four.
visual: Four bars sit at 85 under a dashed line at 88, each shows a 3-point blue gap, and the gaps stack onto a fifth bar that rises to 88 + 12 = 100.
payoff: missing value for a target mean
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Turn every mean into a total and this is easy.

skill: One-variable data: distributions and measures of center and spread
title: Same mean, same range. Which has the bigger standard deviation?
insight: Both have mean 5 and range 8, but standard deviation measures the typical distance from the mean. In the second set four values sit 4 away; in the first only two do, so the second has the larger SD.
visual: Two dot plots stack with the same center line at 5, distance sticks grow from each dot to the center, and the second plot's sticks are longer on average as its readout climbs.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Judge standard deviation by eye, no formula needed.

skill: One-variable data: distributions and measures of center and spread
title: This box plot's right whisker is huge. Does it hold more data?
hook: A box plot's right whisker is three times longer. Does it hold more data?
