insight: No. Each whisker and each half of the box holds about 25% of the data. A long section means those values are spread out, not that there are more of them.
visual: Twenty dots spread along a line, then gather into a box plot with five between each pair of markers; the long right whisker holds the same five dots, just spaced far apart.
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Box plots split data into quarters. Read them right.

skill: One-variable data: distributions and measures of center and spread
title: Mean of 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23 in one second
hook: What is the mean of 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23?
insight: The values are evenly spaced, so they are symmetric around their center and the mean equals the median: (3 + 23) / 2 = 13. Pairing the ends, 3 with 23 and 7 with 19, gives 26 every time.
visual: The dots on the number line fold in half like paper around 13, each outer dot landing on its partner, and the crease turns blue as the mean.
payoff: mean and median of symmetric data
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Symmetric data? The middle is the mean.

skill: One-variable data: distributions and measures of center and spread
title: Two classes peak at 80. One has a long tail. Which mean is higher?
hook: Same peak at 80, but one tail stretches to 40. Which mean is higher?
insight: The one without the tail. The tallest bar is only the most common score; the mean balances all the data, so the tail toward 40 drags that class's mean below its peak.
visual: Two histograms with identical peaks share one axis, a fulcrum under each slides to its balance point, and the tailed one's fulcrum slips left toward the tail.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. The tallest bar isn't the mean. Compare distributions right.

title: Which scatterplot has the stronger association? Not the steeper one
hook: One cloud is steep and scattered, one is shallow and tight. Which is stronger?
insight: Strength is how tightly the points hug a line, not how steep the line is. The shallow, tight cloud has the stronger association.
visual: Two scatterplots sit side by side, residual sticks appear in both, the steep cloud's sticks are long and the shallow cloud's are short, and the label stronger lands on the shallow one.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Steep doesn't mean strong. See the difference.

title: How many points must a line of best fit pass through? Zero
hook: How many data points must a line of best fit pass through?
insight: None. The line is placed to keep the overall vertical gaps small, balancing points above and below it, so it can miss every single point and still be the best fit.
visual: A line pivots through a cloud of dots, residual sticks above and below grow and shrink, and it settles where the sticks balance, touching no dot at all.
payoff: what a line of best fit is
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. A best-fit line isn't connect-the-dots. Here's why.

title: Read a best-fit line's slope in 5 seconds
hook: Find the slope of this best-fit line without touching a single data point.
insight: Pick two places where the line itself crosses grid corners, like (0, 12) and (10, 32), and ignore the dots. The slope is (32 - 12) / 10 = 2.
visual: The dots fade to gray, two grid-corner crossings on the line light up blue, and a slope triangle drops between them reading rise 20 over run 10.
payoff: best-fit line equations from a graph
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Get the best-fit slope fast and skip the dots.

title: Linear, quadratic or exponential? Read the scatterplot's shape
hook: Three scatterplots: straight, bending upward faster, rising then falling. Which model each?
insight: Constant steps fit a line, growth by a fixed ratio that keeps speeding up fits an exponential, and a rise that turns around fits a quadratic. The shape of the cloud chooses the model before any algebra.
visual: One cloud of dots morphs through three shapes while a matching curve, a line, then an exponential, then a parabola, draws itself through each.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Pick the right model at a glance.

title: Test day: before you trust your math, look at the graph
hook: Your answer is 190. The graph tops out at 30. Look again.
insight: SAT figures are drawn to scale unless the question says otherwise, so eyeballing is a legitimate check. If y = 1.5x + 4 gave you 190 at x = 10, you slipped a decimal: the line at 10 sits near 19.
visual: A computed readout of 190 appears beside a scatterplot whose axis ends at 30, a dashed guide from x = 10 meets the line near 19, and 190 is struck as 19 turns blue.
urgent_hook: {test} is today. Check every graph answer by eye.

title: 50% chance of rain Saturday and Sunday. Is rain certain?
hook: 50% chance of rain Saturday, 50% Sunday. Chance it rains this weekend?
insight: Not 100%. Find the chance of no rain at all, 0.5 x 0.5 = 0.25, and subtract from 1: a 75% chance of rain, if the two days are independent.
visual: A square splits into four equal cells for Saturday by Sunday, the three cells with any rain turn blue, and the dry-dry corner stays white as 75% appears.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Probabilities don't just add. Here's the 75% surprise.

title: 12 of 30 marbles are red. How many reds to add to make it half?
hook: 12 of 30 marbles are red. Add reds until half are red. How many?
insight: Each red you add also grows the total, so 3 is wrong. Solve (12 + x)/(30 + x) = 1/2: 24 + 2x = 30 + x, so x = 6, giving 18 red out of 36.
visual: A bar of 30 cells with 12 blue grows one blue cell at a time, the total grows with it, and the half mark slides right until the blue meets it at 18 of 36.
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Adding to the top adds to the bottom too.

title: Roll two dice. Why is 7 the most likely sum?
hook: Roll two dice. Which sum is most likely, and how likely?
insight: The 11 possible sums aren't equally likely; the 36 ordered pairs are. Six pairs make 7, the long diagonal of the 6-by-6 grid, so P(7) = 6/36 = 1/6.
visual: A 6-by-6 grid of dice pairs fills in, each diagonal shades by its sum, and the longest diagonal of six cells lights up blue as 7.
payoff: simple probability with equally likely outcomes
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Count equally likely outcomes, not answer labels.

title: Five heads in a row. Is tails due?
hook: A fair coin lands heads five times in a row. Is tails due?
insight: No. The coin has no memory, so the next flip is still 1/2. Five heads in a row was unlikely beforehand, 1/32, but once it has happened it doesn't change the next flip.
visual: Five coins land heads in a row and fade to gray, a fresh coin spins alone on a clean page, and its probability chip reads 1/2 in blue.
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Coins have no memory. Neither does a probability question.

skill: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error
title: To halve a poll's margin of error, how many more people?
hook: Poll of 400, margin 5%. How many people for a 2.5% margin?
insight: About 1,600, four times as many. The margin shrinks with the square root of the sample size, so halving it takes four times the people: bigger random samples mean smaller margins, but slowly.
visual: Sample estimates scatter as dots around a true value; the sample-size counter jumps from 400 to 1,600 and the cloud's spread tightens to exactly half.
payoff: sample size and margin of error
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Bigger sample, smaller margin. Here's how much smaller.

skill: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error
title: 24% plus or minus 3% of 1,500 students. What's the plausible count?
hook: A sample says 24% bike, margin 3%. School of 1,500. Plausible range?
insight: Apply both ends of the interval to the population: 21% to 27% of 1,500 is 315 to 405 students. Saying exactly 360 ignores the margin of error.
visual: A bracket from 21% to 27% stretches over a 1,500-dot school, its two ends drop guide lines to the counts 315 and 405, and 360 sits in the middle.
payoff: population estimates with a margin of error
urgent_hook: Retaking on {date}? Hard-module inference uses both ends of the interval.

skill: Evaluating statistical claims: observational studies and experiments
title: More firefighters, more fire damage. Should we send fewer?
hook: Fires with more firefighters cause more damage. Should we send fewer firefighters?
insight: No. Bigger fires draw more firefighters and cause more damage, so fire size is a lurking variable driving both. A correlation can come from a third variable instead of cause.
visual: Two rising bars, firefighters and damage, sit side by side; a hidden third bar, fire size, slides in beneath them and arrows grow from it to both.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Spot the hidden third variable in any study.

skill: Evaluating statistical claims: observational studies and experiments
title: 70% got better on the new drug. Does the drug work?
hook: Everyone got the new cold drug, and 70% felt better in a week. Works?
insight: You can't tell: most colds get better in a week anyway. Without a randomly assigned comparison group, there is nothing to measure the drug against.
visual: A single group bar reaches 70%, then a second bar for an untreated group rises beside it to a similar height, and only the gap between them, the drug's real effect, turns blue.
payoff: why experiments need a control group
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. No comparison group, no conclusion. Here's why.

skill: Evaluating statistical claims: observational studies and experiments
title: Students with tutors have lower grades. Do tutors hurt?
hook: Students who have tutors have lower grades on average. Do tutors hurt?
insight: Probably not: students with low grades are the ones who get tutors. The arrow can point the other way, so an observational link can't tell you which causes which.
visual: An arrow from tutor to lower grades draws itself, pauses, then swings around to point from lower grades to tutor as the original arrow is struck.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Causation arrows can point backward. Spot it.

title: Area from coordinates without any formula
hook: Triangle with corners (0, 0), (6, 2) and (2, 5). What is its area?
insight: Box it in a 6 by 5 rectangle of area 30, then subtract the three right triangles around it, 6, 6 and 5. The area is 30 - 17 = 13.
visual: A rectangle draws itself around the tilted triangle on a grid, the three corner triangles shade and slide off one by one, and the leftover triangle is labeled 13 in blue.
payoff: Area of a polygon from coordinates
urgent_hook: Retaking on {date}? Area from coordinates is a hard-module favorite. Box it in.

title: The one cube whose volume equals its surface area
hook: Which cube has the same number for its volume and surface area?
insight: Edge 6: the volume is 6^3 = 216 and the surface area is 6 x 6^2 = 216. Setting s^3 = 6s^2 gives s = 6, because a cube has six faces.
visual: A cube grows edge by edge while two mono readouts, volume and surface area, race each other and cross exactly at 216.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. One cube makes volume and surface area tie. Which?

title: Three face areas. Can you find the volume?
hook: A box's faces have areas 12, 15 and 20. What is its volume?
insight: Multiply the three areas: lw x lh x wh = (lwh)^2 = 3600, so the volume is sqrt(3600) = 60. The box is 3 by 4 by 5.
visual: Three faces of a wireframe box light up with 12, 15 and 20, their product stacks into 3600, and the square root collapses it into a 3 by 4 by 5 box.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Three faces multiply into the volume squared.

title: Slant height is for the skin, height is for the filling
hook: Pyramid: base 10, height 12, slant height 13. Which number goes where?
insight: Volume fills the inside, so it uses the vertical height: 1/3 x 100 x 12 = 400. Surface area wraps the outside, so its triangles use the slant height: 100 + 4 x 1/2 x 10 x 13 = 360.
visual: The pyramid fills with water up its vertical height, then its four faces peel open like petals, each triangle labeled with the slant height 13.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Height fills, slant height wraps. Never swap them.

title: Same fence: square pen or round pen?
hook: 40 meters of fence. Square pen or circular pen: which encloses more?
insight: The circle, about 127 square meters against the square's 100. With perimeter 40 the square has side 10, and the circle has radius 20/pi and area 400/pi.
visual: A square loop of rope relaxes into a circle while the area readout climbs from 100 to about 127.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Same perimeter, different area. Guess first.

title: A hexagon is six triangles in disguise
hook: A regular hexagon has sides of 2. What is its area?
insight: Lines to the center cut it into six equilateral triangles of side 2, each with area sqrt3. The hexagon is 6sqrt3, about 10.4.
visual: Six equilateral triangles fly in and lock around a center point into a hexagon, the area chip counting sqrt3 six times.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Every regular hexagon is six equilateral triangles.

title: Which angle sum is impossible?
hook: Parallel lines, one angle 50. Which sum is impossible: 100, 180, 230, 260?
insight: Every angle is 50 or 130, so any two of them add to 100, 180 or 260. 230 is impossible.
visual: The eight angles collapse into two chips, 50 and 130, the three possible pair sums light up, and 230 is struck in blue.
payoff: Could NOT questions with parallel lines
urgent_hook: Retaking on {date}? This could-NOT angle question lives in the hard module.

title: Sides 3 and 7. How many whole-number third sides?
hook: Two sides are 3 and 7. How many whole numbers work for the third?
insight: Five: 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9. The third side must be longer than 7 - 3 = 4 and shorter than 7 + 3 = 10.
visual: A hinge with arms 3 and 7 opens from flat to flat, and the third side's readout sweeps from 4 to 10 without touching either end.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. The third side lives between difference and sum.

title: Draw one extra line and the bend angle appears
hook: Two parallel lines and a zigzag making 30 and 45 degrees. The bend?
insight: 75. Draw a third parallel line through the bend: it splits the bend into two alternate angles, 30 and 45.
visual: A dashed parallel line slides in through the bend and splits it, and the 30 and 45 copy across from the outer lines into the two halves.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Stuck on a bend? Draw one more parallel line.

title: Regular polygon angles: go around the outside
hook: Each interior angle of a regular polygon is 140. How many sides?
insight: Each exterior angle is 180 - 140 = 40, and the exterior angles of any polygon add to 360, so it has 360 / 40 = 9 sides.
visual: A point walks around the polygon turning 40 degrees at each corner, and the turns gather at the center into one full circle of nine wedges.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Exterior angles always total 360.

title: The longest stick that fits in a box
hook: A 3 by 4 by 12 box. Longest stick that fits inside?
insight: 13, by Pythagoras twice: the floor diagonal is 5 (3-4-5), then 5 and 12 make 13 (5-12-13).
visual: The floor diagonal draws across the base, then a blue line rises from its end to the far top corner, each right triangle lighting up in turn.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Use Pythagoras twice for the box diagonal.

title: sin^2(23) + sin^2(67), no calculator
hook: No calculator: what is sin^2(23) + sin^2(67)?
insight: Exactly 1. sin 67 = cos 23 because 23 + 67 = 90, and sin^2 + cos^2 = 1 is Pythagoras in a right triangle with hypotenuse 1.
visual: A right triangle with hypotenuse 1 shows legs sin 23 and cos 23, squares grow on both legs and slide onto the hypotenuse square, filling it exactly.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Five seconds, no calculator. Can you?

title: Radians to degrees in one move
hook: Convert 5pi/6 radians to degrees in two seconds.
insight: pi radians is 180 degrees, so replace pi with 180: 5 x 180 / 6 = 150 degrees. To go back, multiply degrees by pi/180.
visual: The pi in 5pi/6 flips over like a tile into 180, the fraction resolves to 150, and a ray swings to 150 degrees on a circle.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Swap pi for 180 and you are done.

title: Do these two circles touch?
hook: Do x^2 + y^2 = 25 and (x-6)^2 + y^2 = 1 touch?
insight: Yes, at exactly one point, (5, 0). The centers are 6 apart and the radii add to 5 + 1 = 6.
visual: Both circles draw, a dashed segment links the centers and splits into a 5 and a 1, and the single touching point at (5, 0) lights up.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Center distance versus radii. That's the test.

title: The 2018 SAT that was too easy, and why scores fell
hook: In June 2018 the SAT was easy. Students got lower scores than expected. Why?
insight: Each test form is equated so a score means the same on every date; when the June 2, 2018 form came out unusually easy, the scale got steep at the top, and by prep-company counts a single math miss could cost about 30 points. College Board stood by the scores.
visual: Two raw-to-scaled curves draw on one grid, a typical form and the June 2018 form; the June curve drops steeply near the top, and a dot for one missed question slides down it while a mono readout falls by about 30.
urgent_hook: Scores for {test} are out. Here is what happened the year an easy SAT hurt.

title: Divide any number from 1 to 10 by 11 in one second
hook: What is 7 divided by 11? You already know it.
insight: 0.636363...: 1/11 = 9/99, so n/11 = 9n/99, and anything over 99 just repeats its two digits. 7 x 9 = 63, so 7/11 = 0.6363...
visual: The fraction 7/11 morphs to 63/99 as top and bottom both multiply by 9, then 63 copies itself endlessly along a decimal tape.
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. A one-second division trick for your typed answers.

title: What is 2^100 - 2^99? Not 2.
hook: Two to the 100th minus two to the 99th. What's left?
insight: 2^99. 2^100 is two copies of 2^99, so taking one copy away leaves one. The common wrong answer, 2^1 = 2, subtracts the exponents.
visual: A bar labeled 2^100 splits into two equal halves labeled 2^99, one half slides off the page, and the struck answer 2^1 fades beside the remaining half.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. One exponent trap to kill before test day.

title: The 1980 SAT question that forgot negative numbers
hook: Which list has the square of an integer and the cube of another?
insight: On the October 1980 SAT a second row also worked, because 4 = (-2)^2 and 8 = 2^3 use two different integers once negatives count. Michael Galligan, 17, of New York, challenged the key, and ETS rescored the question.
visual: Two rows of numbers sit on the page; in the second row 8 = 2^3 inks first, 4 = 2^2 is struck because 2 is reused, then 4 = (-2)^2 slides in from the negative side of a number line and the row lights in accent.
payoff: the 'all variables are real numbers' habit: check negatives
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. One student beat the SAT by remembering negatives.

title: 60 mph there, 40 mph back. Your average is not 50.
hook: Drive there at 60 mph, back at 40 mph. Average speed?
insight: 48 mph. Average speed is total distance over total time, and you spend longer at 40: for 120 miles each way that's 240 miles in 2 + 3 = 5 hours.
visual: Two trip bars have equal length, but the 40 mph bar takes 3 time blocks to the 60 mph bar's 2; the blocks pool into one line of 5 and the readout settles on 48, with 50 struck beside it.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. This average trap fools almost everyone.

title: A bat and a ball cost $1.10. The ball is not 10 cents.
hook: A bat and ball cost $1.10. The bat costs $1 more. Ball?
insight: 5 cents. Call the ball b and the bat b + 1, so 2b + 1 = 1.10 and b = 0.05. Ten cents fails: the bat would be $1.10 and the total $1.20.
visual: Two bars, ball and bat, where the bat bar is the ball bar plus a $1 block; the $1 block lifts off, leaving two equal ball bars sharing 10 cents.
payoff: writing a system from a word problem
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Read this word problem slowly; that's the whole lesson.

title: Square any number ending in 5 instantly: 65^2 = 4225
hook: 65 squared. Under three seconds.
insight: 4225. Multiply the tens digit by the next number up and attach 25: 6 x 7 = 42. Why: move a 5-wide strip from one side to the other and 65^2 = 60 x 70 + 5^2.
visual: A 65 by 65 square has a 5-wide strip sliced off its top and moved to its side, leaving a 60 by 70 rectangle plus one lone 5 by 5 corner square.
payoff: mental arithmetic and the difference of squares
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Square numbers ending in 5 without the calculator.

title: 6 / 2(1 + 2): is it 1 or 9?
hook: 6 / 2(1 + 2). Is the answer 1 or 9?
insight: 9 by the standard convention: multiplication and division go left to right, so 6/2 = 3, then 3 x 3 = 9. The fight exists only because the notation is ambiguous, which is why careful tests write a stacked fraction instead.
visual: The expression sits in ink and splits into two readings, 6 over 2(1 + 2) = 1 and (6/2)(1 + 2) = 9; the second lights in accent as the left-to-right reading, and the first fades with a label 'needs brackets'.
payoff: order of operations in equivalent expressions
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Settle the viral order-of-operations fight in one picture.

title: How many squares are on a chessboard? Not 64.
hook: How many squares are on a chessboard?
insight: 204. Count by size: 64 of size 1, 49 of size 2, 36 of size 3, down to 1 of size 8, so 1 + 4 + 9 + ... + 64 = 204.
visual: A chessboard draws in ink, then a 1x1 window, a 2x2 window and larger windows slide across it, leaving their counts 64, 49, 36 ... 1 stacked in a mono column that sums to 204.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Count carefully; this one rewards organized thinking.

title: 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 512. One less than the next power
hook: 1 plus 2 plus 4, doubling up to 512. Total?
insight: 1023, which is 2^10 - 1. Each new block exactly fills the gap the last ones left, so the running total is always one less than the next power of 2.
visual: Blocks of 1, 2, 4 and 8 slide into a row of length 16 leaving a single empty cell each time, the pattern repeating up to 512 and a mono readout landing on 1023 = 1024 - 1.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Doubling, summed, in one line of blocks.

title: One pipe fills a tank in 3 hours, another in 6. Together?
hook: Pipe A fills a tank in 3 hours, pipe B in 6. Together?
insight: 2 hours, not 4.5. Rates add but times don't: A fills 1/3 of the tank per hour and B fills 1/6, so together 1/3 + 1/6 = 1/2 tank per hour, which takes 2 hours.
visual: A tank fills in two shades, a third per hour from A and a sixth from B, the slices stacking into a half tank per hour while a clock stops at 2 and 4.5 is struck in blue.
payoff: rate word problems and rational equations
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Add rates, never times; here is why.

title: A 10-meter fence, a post every 2 meters. How many posts?

title: You will see an SAT question that does not ask for x

title: You will see an "each additional" question. Here's the reverse
hook: $8 for the first pound, $3 each additional. The bill is $41. Pounds?

urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. This hard-module pattern keeps coming back.

title: This scary slope formula is just a staircase
hook: m = (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1). It looks scary. It's a staircase.
insight: The little 1 and 2 just name the first and second point. The top is how far up you went, the bottom is how far over: rise over run.
visual: Two dots appear, one stair step connects them, its height labels itself y2 - y1 and its width x2 - x1, and the subscripts fade as the fraction becomes rise over run.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. The slope formula is one stair step.

title: Point-slope form is just the slope formula, multiplied out
hook: y - y1 = m(x - x1). Where did this come from?
insight: The slope from a fixed point (x1, y1) to any point (x, y) on the line is m: (y - y1)/(x - x1) = m. Multiply both sides by (x - x1) and you have point-slope form.
visual: The slope fraction sits between one fixed dot and one moving dot, the denominator slides across the equals sign to multiply m, and the result reads y - y1 = m(x - x1).
payoff: line through a point with a given slope
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Write any line from one point and a slope.

skill: Systems of two linear equations in two variables

urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Expect a no-solution system. Here's the fast read.

skill: Linear inequalities in one or two variables
title: You will see "What is the greatest number of..." on the SAT
hook: Greatest whole number of items? Solve, then test both neighbors.
insight: Solve the inequality as an equation, then plug the two whole numbers on either side of the boundary back into the story: the one that fits while its neighbor breaks the limit is the answer, with no rounding guesswork.
visual: A number line marks a boundary at 10.625, the neighbors 10 and 11 are plugged back into the story, 10 lights blue with a check and 11 is struck.
payoff: max and min whole-number inequality questions
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Expect a greatest-whole-number question. Test both neighbors.

title: What does 16^(3/4) even mean?
hook: 16 to the three-fourths. What does a fraction in the exponent even mean?
insight: The bottom of the fraction is a root and the top is a power: 16^(3/4) = (fourth root of 16)^3 = 2^3 = 8. Take the root first to keep the numbers small.
visual: The exponent 3/4 splits apart, the 4 drops into a root sign around 16 and shrinks it to 2, then the 3 lifts it to 8 in accent.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Fraction exponents look scary. They're two small steps.

title: This scary fraction is just a line with a hole
hook: x squared minus 1, over x minus 1. What does this graph look like?
insight: Factor the top: (x - 1)(x + 1)/(x - 1) = x + 1 for every x except 1. The graph is the line y = x + 1 with one missing point at (1, 2).
visual: The fraction's top splits into two factors, one (x - 1) cancels the bottom, and a straight line draws itself with a small open circle at (1, 2).
payoff: Simplifying rational expressions by canceling factors
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Scary fractions often hide a simple line.

skill: Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables
title: You will see a 'no real solutions' question on the SAT
hook: x^2 - 6x + c = 0 has no real solutions. Which c works?
insight: No real solutions means the discriminant is negative: 36 - 4c < 0, so c > 9. Picture the parabola lifted completely off the x-axis.
visual: The parabola rises as c increases, touches the axis at c = 9, then lifts free, and the inequality c > 9 writes itself in blue.
payoff: Number of solutions from the discriminant
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Expect a discriminant question. Here's the fast read.

skill: Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables
title: You will see 'what is the positive solution' on the SAT
hook: x^2 + 2x - 24 = 0. What is the positive solution?
insight: Factor into (x + 6)(x - 4) = 0, so x = -6 or 4. The question asks for the positive one, 4; the other root, -6, is the trap.
visual: The parabola crosses the axis at -6 and 4, the word positive underlines itself, and the -6 crossing fades while 4 lights up in blue.
payoff: Solving quadratics and answering the asked root
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Circle the word 'positive' before you solve.

title: This negative exponent is just halving: 80 times 2^(-x)
hook: 80 times 2 to the negative x. Growth or decay?
insight: 2^(-x) = (1/2)^x, so the function is 80(1/2)^x, which halves every time x goes up by 1: 80, 40, 20, 10. A minus sign in the exponent turns growth into decay.
visual: The curve 80 times 2^x mirrors across the y-axis into a falling curve, and the outputs 80, 40, 20, 10 print in mono as x steps up.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. A negative exponent can hide a decay model.

title: You will see 'which equation matches this graph' on the SAT
hook: Four equations, one graph. Which one matches it?
insight: Check the y-intercept first, since it usually eliminates two choices at once. Then test one clear point, like the vertex or an x-intercept, to pick between the last two.
visual: A parabola sits on the grid, a probe at x = 0 strikes two equations whose intercepts miss, then a second probe at the vertex strikes the third.
payoff: Matching equations to graphs and tables
urgent_hook: {test} on {date} will show a graph and four equations. Here's the two-point test.

skill: One-variable data: distributions and measures of center and spread
title: You will see a dot plot mean question. Count every dot
hook: A dot plot: five 1s, three 2s, two 3s. What is the mean?
insight: Every dot is a data value, so add value times frequency: 5(1) + 3(2) + 2(3) = 17 over 10 dots, a mean of 1.7. Averaging the labels 1, 2, 3 gives 2, which is wrong.
visual: Stacked dots drop one by one onto a number line, a fulcrum slides under them and balances at 1.7, and the struck 2 sits at the middle label.
payoff: mean from a dot plot or frequency table
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. You will see a dot plot. Count every dot.

skill: One-variable data: distributions and measures of center and spread
title: The standard deviation formula is just an average square
hook: This scary formula is just the side of an average square.
insight: Square each distance from the mean, average those squares, then take the square root: SD is the side length of the average square. For 1, 5, 9 the squares are 16, 0, 16, averaging 32/3, so SD = sqrt(32/3), about 3.3.
visual: Distance sticks from each dot to the mean grow into blue squares, the squares melt into one average square, and its side slides down onto the number line as the SD.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Stop fearing the SD formula. It's one square.

skill: One-variable data: distributions and measures of center and spread
title: x-bar = (sum of x) / n is just leveling the bars
hook: x-bar equals sigma x over n. That symbol pile means one thing.
insight: Sigma means add them all up, and dividing by n shares the total equally. For 2, 4 and 9 the total 15 split 3 ways gives 5: the mean is the height every bar would have if they were made equal.
visual: Three bars of heights 2, 4 and 9 pour their tops into the shorter bars until all three level at 5, and the symbol x-bar settles on the level line.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. That sigma symbol is just a total. Here's proof.

title: You will see a line of best fit question. Use the line, not the dot
hook: Best-fit line: y = 2.5x + 10. Predict y at x = 8.
insight: A predicted value comes from the line, not from a data point: 2.5(8) + 10 = 30. A dot sitting at (8, 34) is the actual value, and choosing 34 is the trap.
visual: A scatterplot with its line; a dashed guide rises from x = 8 to the line and across to 30 in blue, while the nearby dot at 34 is struck.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. You'll predict from a best-fit line. Use the line.

title: The SAT rarely says 'given.' Spot the hidden condition
hook: 'If a student is selected from those who own a dog...' That's a given.
insight: Phrases like selected from those who, among the, or of the name the group that becomes your denominator. Find that group's total in the table before you read anything else.
visual: A sentence types across the page, the phrase from those who own a dog underlines itself in blue, and the matching table row lifts out with its total circled.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. You'll see this wording. Know the denominator instantly.

title: You will see this rectangle-plus-semicircle on the SAT
hook: A 10 by 6 rectangle with a semicircle on the short side. Area?
insight: Split it into reference-sheet shapes: the rectangle is 60, and the semicircle has diameter 6, radius 3 and area 9pi/2. The total is 60 + 4.5pi, about 74.1.
visual: A dashed line splits the figure, the rectangle and the half-disk slide apart to get their own area chips, then slide back together as the chips add.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. A split-and-add figure like this is almost certain.

title: You will see Pythagoras hiding in a rectangle
hook: A rectangle has a diagonal of 13 and a side of 5. Area?
insight: The diagonal makes a right triangle with two sides, so the other side is 12 (5-12-13) and the area is 60.
visual: A diagonal cuts the rectangle, one half lifts away as a right triangle, the missing leg reads 12, and the rectangle refills with area 60.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. A diagonal in a rectangle is a hypotenuse.

title: The distance formula is just Pythagoras
hook: sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2). Where does that come from?
insight: Draw the right triangle under the segment: the legs are the horizontal and vertical gaps, and the distance is the hypotenuse. From (1, 1) to (4, 5) the legs are 3 and 4, so the distance is 5.
visual: The formula sits at the top while a dashed right triangle drops beneath a segment on a grid, and each piece of the formula maps onto a leg.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. The distance formula is a triangle in disguise.

title: You will see this trig ratio question on the SAT
hook: cos A = 8/17 in a right triangle. What is tan A?
insight: Draw the triangle the ratio describes, adjacent 8 and hypotenuse 17. The missing side is 15 from the 8-15-17 triple, so tan A = 15/8.
visual: The fraction 8/17 unfolds into a right triangle with those two sides, the third side fills in as 15, and 15/8 lights up.
payoff: One trig ratio given, find another
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Turn one ratio into a triangle, then read any other.

title: You will see a circle with a missing constant
hook: x^2 + y^2 - 4x + 2y = k has radius 5. Find k.
insight: Completing the squares adds 4 and 1, so the right side becomes k + 5, which must equal r^2 = 25. So k = 20.
visual: The 4 and the 1 drop onto the right side next to k, and a slider on k grows the circle until its radius reaches 5 at k = 20.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Expect a circle with an unknown constant.

skill: Systems of two linear equations in two variables
title: Solve any SAT system by tapping one point in Desmos

visual: Drawn in our style: two lines draw on, a blue dot pulses where they cross, and the coordinate chip reads (8, 3).
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Practice this one tap before it.

skill: Systems of two linear equations in two variables
title: Find the no-solution k by sliding until the lines never meet
hook: 5x-2y=3 and kx-4y=9. Which k means no solution?
insight: Make k a slider in Desmos; as k moves, the intersection slides away, and at k = 10 the lines go parallel with no crossing. The algebra agrees: 5/10 = 2/4, but 3/9 is not 1/2.
visual: Drawn in our style: a slider chip ticks k upward, the crossing dot races off the page, and at k = 10 the two lines run parallel.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. One slider answers the hardest system question.

skill: Systems of two linear equations in two variables
title: These lines look parallel in Desmos. They cross at x = 100

insight: The slopes differ, so the lines cross exactly once, at (100, 51), far off the default screen. Compare slopes exactly instead of trusting the picture.
visual: Drawn in our style: two lines look parallel near the origin, then the view zooms out until they meet at (100, 51) under a blue dot.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Don't trust an unzoomed graph on it.

title: Why 6/sqrt(3) is secretly 2sqrt(3)
hook: Which is equivalent to 6 over the square root of 3?
insight: 6 is 2 times 3, and 3 is sqrt(3) times sqrt(3), so one sqrt(3) cancels and 6/sqrt(3) = 2sqrt(3), about 3.46. Multiplying top and bottom by sqrt(3) gives the same answer.
visual: The 6 on top splits into 2, sqrt(3) and sqrt(3), one sqrt(3) glides down to cancel the bottom, and 2sqrt(3) remains in accent.
payoff: Rationalizing denominators to match answer choices
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Match radical answer choices in five seconds.

skill: Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables
title: 8^x = 4^(x+1): rewrite both sides as powers of 2
hook: 8^x = 4^(x+1). What is x?
insight: Write both sides as powers of 2: 2^(3x) = 2^(2x + 2), and equal bases mean equal exponents, so 3x = 2x + 2 and x = 2. Check: 8^2 = 64 = 4^3.
visual: 8 and 4 morph into 2^3 and 2^2, the matching bases fade, and the exponents drop into a one-line linear equation that resolves to x = 2.
payoff: Exponential equations with a common base
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Same base, then match exponents. That's the whole trick.

skill: Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables
title: x^3 + 3x^2 - 4x - 12 = 0 factors in two moves
hook: Solve x cubed plus 3x squared minus 4x minus 12 equals 0.
insight: Group in pairs: x^2(x + 3) - 4(x + 3) = (x^2 - 4)(x + 3) = (x - 2)(x + 2)(x + 3). The solutions are 2, -2 and -3.
visual: The four terms split into two pairs, each pair pulls out its own factor, the shared (x + 3) slides out front in blue, and the graph confirms three crossings.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Four terms? Group them in pairs.

title: Check 'which is equivalent' by stacking two graphs
hook: Which is equivalent to 2x minus 3, squared, minus 4x squared?
insight: Graph the question and each choice, since equivalent expressions draw the identical curve. Here the 'quadratic' turns out to be the line -12x + 9, and only that choice lands on it.
visual: The question's graph draws itself as a straight line, each answer choice draws over it in blue, and only -12x + 9 lands exactly on top.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Let the graph check your algebra.

skill: Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables
title: x^2 + kx + 9 = 0 has one solution. There are two k's
hook: x^2 + kx + 9 = 0 has exactly one solution. What is k?
insight: Put k on a slider: the parabola touches the axis exactly once at k = -6 and again at k = 6. The discriminant k^2 - 36 = 0 confirms both.
visual: A parabola drifts and rises as the k slider moves, kisses the axis at k = -6, lifts off, then comes back down to kiss it again at k = 6, each touch marked in blue.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. 'Exactly one solution' can hide two answers.

title: Find 35% of 60 in your head with 10% blocks
hook: What is 35% of 60? No calculator, three seconds.
insight: 10% is the number with the decimal moved one place, 6, and 5% is half of that, 3. Then 35% = 10% + 10% + 10% + 5%, so 6 + 6 + 6 + 3 = 21.
visual: A 60-bar splits into ten 6-unit blocks, three blocks and a half block slide out in blue, and their labels 6, 6, 6, 3 add to 21.
payoff: percent of a quantity, fast checks
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Check percent answers in your head with this.

title: 10 L of drink is 30% juice. How much water makes it 20%?
hook: 10 liters of drink is 30% juice. Add how much water to make 20%?
insight: The juice never changes: it is 3 liters. For 3 liters to be 20% of the drink, the total must be 3 / 0.2 = 15 liters, so add 5 liters of water.
visual: A glass shows a 3-liter blue juice layer under 7 liters of water; water pours in, the glass grows to 15 liters, and the fixed blue layer shrinks from 30% to 20% of the height.
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. In mixture questions, find the part that never changes.

title: 37.5% of 64 is easy once you see it's 3/8
hook: What is 37.5% of 64? It's a fraction in disguise.
visual: A circle of 64 dots splits into 8 slices of 8, each slice tagged 12.5%, and three slices turn blue to show 24.
payoff: percent of a quantity with friendly fractions
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Spot the fraction hiding inside a percent.

title: 8% tax and a 20% tip: when do you just add the percents?
hook: A $40 meal, 8% tax, 20% tip on the pre-tax price. Total?
insight: Both percents are of the same $40, so they add: 40 x 1.28 = $51.20. If the tip were on the taxed total they would multiply: 40 x 1.08 x 1.2 = $51.84.
visual: Two blue slices, $3.20 and $8, attach to the same $40 bar side by side; then the tip slice regrows on the taller taxed bar to $8.64 and the two totals stack for comparison.
payoff: tax and tip on different bases
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Check which amount each percent is of.

title: A pie chart slice is 72 degrees. What percent is that?
hook: A pie chart slice measures 72 degrees. What percent of the whole is it?
insight: The full circle, 360 degrees, is 100%, so every 3.6 degrees is 1%. 72 / 360 = 0.2, so the slice is 20%.
visual: A circle fills sweep by sweep into five equal 72-degree wedges, one wedge stays blue, and the readout 72/360 morphs into 20%.
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Turn any slice into a percent with one division.

skill: Ratios, rates, proportional relationships, and units
title: Add 5 to both numbers and 1:2 becomes 2:3. Find them
hook: Numbers in ratio 1:2 become 2:3 when you add 5 to each. Find them.
insight: Call them x and 2x. Then (x + 5)/(2x + 5) = 2/3 gives 3x + 15 = 4x + 10, so x = 5: the numbers are 5 and 10. Adding the same amount changes a ratio; only multiplying keeps it.
visual: Bars of 1 and 2 units each grow by the same blue 5-block, and the 1:2 label morphs to 2:3 as the bars settle at 10 and 15.
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Adding to a ratio changes it. Watch this.

skill: Ratios, rates, proportional relationships, and units
title: A 1:50,000 map scale has no units. That's the whole trick
hook: On a 1:50,000 map, two towns are 4 cm apart. How far really?
insight: A scale ratio has no units: 1 cm on paper is 50,000 cm in the world. 4 cm is 200,000 cm, which is 2,000 meters, or 2 kilometers.
visual: A 4 cm ruler segment on the map stretches across the page as its label multiplies by 50,000, then the long number 200,000 cm drops zeros into 2 km.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. A map scale is just one unit conversion.

skill: Ratios, rates, proportional relationships, and units
title: Rate questions with letters? Plug in small numbers
hook: A machine fills 87 bottles in m minutes. How many in 12k minutes?
insight: The rate is 87/m bottles per minute, so 12k minutes gives 1,044k/m. To check fast, try m = 3 and k = 1: 29 bottles a minute for 12 minutes is 348, and only the right choice gives 348.
visual: m becomes 3 and k becomes 1 in every answer choice, each evaluates in place, and only 1,044k/m lands on 348 while the others strike through.
urgent_hook: {days} days to {test}. Letters in a rate question? Swap in small numbers and test.

title: 90th percentile does not mean you got 90% right

urgent_hook: Scores are out and {test} is {days} days away. Read your percentile right.

urgent_hook: {test} is in {days} days. Let the graph solve it and skip the fake answers.

title: Are these expressions equivalent? Graph them and look
hook: Is (x + 2)^2 - 4 the same as x(x + 4)?
insight: Yes. Equivalent means equal for every x, so the two graphs are one curve: (x + 2)^2 - 4 and x(x + 4) land exactly on top of each other, while a nonequivalent choice like x^2 + 4 peels away.

urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. If two graphs merge, the expressions are equivalent.

title: What does the little 3 on a root sign mean?
hook: What does the tiny 3 on this root sign do?
insight: It asks for the number that, used three times, makes the inside: the cube root of 64 is 4. Unlike square roots it works on negatives too, so the cube root of -27 is -3.
visual: A 4-by-4-by-4 cube of blocks builds out of 64, then a -27 cube builds in the negative direction with side -3, and the little index 3 glows in blue.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. The little 3 on a root sign, explained in one cube.

title: This scary root is just x + 3 in disguise
hook: What is the square root of x squared plus 6x plus 9?
insight: The inside is a perfect square, (x + 3)^2, so the root is |x + 3|, which equals x + 3 whenever x is at least -3. Look for a perfect square under a root first.
visual: The trinomial under the root reassembles into a square of side x + 3, the root sign peels it down to its side length, and the side reads x + 3.
urgent_hook: {test} is {days} days away. Under the root, look for a perfect square.

title: You will see 'linear or exponential?' on the SAT. Here's the tell
hook: Grows by 3 each year, or by 3% each year. Which is exponential?
insight: The same amount each step is linear; the same percent each step is exponential, because 3% of a bigger number is bigger. Look for 'percent' or 'times' versus a fixed amount.

payoff: Linear versus exponential models in context
urgent_hook: {test} on {date} will ask linear or exponential. Here's the one-word tell.

title: You will see a vertex question in context. Read k as the max
hook: h(t) = -5(t - 2)^2 + 25. What does 25 represent?
insight: In vertex form, 25 is the maximum value of h and 2 is the time it happens, so the object reaches its greatest height, 25, at t = 2. The -5 only sets how sharply the arc bends.
visual: The arc draws over a time axis, a dashed guide from its peak drops to t = 2 and another slides to the height axis at 25, both labeled in mono.
urgent_hook: {days} days until {test}. Vertex form in a word problem? The peak is written in.

title: You will see x-intercepts -3 and 2. Which function is it?
hook: A parabola crosses at -3 and 2 and hits the y-axis at -12.
insight: Zeros at -3 and 2 give y = a(x + 3)(x - 2), and the y-intercept fixes a: a(3)(-2) = -12, so a = 2. The function is y = 2(x + 3)(x - 2).
visual: Two crossing points spawn the factors (x + 3) and (x - 2) in the formula, a probe at x = 0 reads -12, and the parabola stretches until a settles at 2.
payoff: Writing a quadratic from its zeros and a point
urgent_hook: {test} on {date}: expect intercepts and a formula to match. Here's the method.

skill: One-variable data: distributions and measures of center and spread
title: You will see a median from a frequency table. Count to the middle
hook: Values 0 to 4 with frequencies 8, 5, 4, 2, 1. What's the median?
